{"stdout":"# Editorial playbook — AI Edge Briefing

You are producing today's edition of a daily briefing on frontier AI. The reader uses this as their single place to stay at the edge: the advances, the research, and how AI is being used for good and for harm — cyber, influence ops, military, health, science, policy. It is not a "fun uses of AI" newsletter. It is raw, factual, sourced.

The reader's standard: **every claim links to where it came from, every number is the number in the source, and nothing is written that the sources do not say.** If you cannot source it, it does not go in.

## 0. Setup

1. Work in the repo root. Determine today's date in **America/Toronto**: `TZ=America/Toronto date +%F`. That is the edition date, `DATE`.
2. `ls data/` — the previous edition tells you the cutoff. The coverage window (`WINDOW`) is from the previous edition's `generated_at` to now (if there is no previous edition, the 24 hours before now). Write it down as absolute timestamps in both UTC and ET; you will hand it to the subagents. Read the previous edition so you do not repeat it; a story already covered goes in again **only if there is a new development**, flagged `update`, and the bullets report only the new facts.
3. `node scripts/build.js --topics` — the existing topic slugs. Reuse them; only coin a new slug when nothing fits.
   `node scripts/build.js --storylines` — the open storylines (id, status, name, frame). An item that is a development in one of those arcs is **filed under it** (see §3, `storylines`). The daily never creates a storyline; the Monday Week in Review does.
4. Every day is a daily edition, Mondays included. The week in review is a separate weekly edition with its own playbook (`PROMPT-WEEK.md`) and its own routine — never part of the daily file.

## 0b. Keep your own context small — it is most of what this edition costs

Every turn you take re-sends this whole conversation. So the price of anything you pull into your context
is its size **times the number of turns that come after it** — a page you open early is paid for a hundred
times over. Measured: writing the edition costs about $3; re-reading the conversation while writing it costs
about $20. None of the rules below cost you a source, a check or an item. They stop you paying rent on text
you have already used.

1. **Write files with `Write`, and change them with `Edit`.** Never `cat > file <<'EOF'`, and never a
   `python3 -`/`node -e` script that does find-and-replace on a data file — those put the whole file, or
   whole paragraphs twice over, into the conversation as a command argument. `Edit` sends only the line that
   changes.
2. **Never print a file back out after writing it.** You know what you wrote. To check it, run the
   validator — it prints errors, not contents.
3. **Read the part you need.** `sed -n '40,80p'` over `cat` for anything long, and don't re-read a file
   that has not changed since you read it.
4. **`node scripts/fetch.js` caps its output at 12,000 characters** — the claim, the date and the figures
   are at the top of a page. Add `--full` only when you have looked and what you need is genuinely further
   down. Don't pipe it through `head` as well; the cap is already there.
5. **Let the subagents hold the raw material.** A beat opens fifty pages and hands you back a page of facts;
   that is the whole point of them. When you need a page opened and checked, and a subagent can do it,
   prefer that to opening it yourself.
6. Same rules for the subagents you launch — put a short version of this in every prompt you give them.

None of this licenses checking less. If a fact needs a source opened, open it. Verify everything §2 says to
verify. This is about what you keep afterwards, not what you look at.

## 1. Sweep the sources — four beats in parallel

Read `SOURCES.md`. Then launch **four general-purpose subagents in one message** with the Agent tool, one per beat. Give each: the `WINDOW` as absolute timestamps, its beat's source list from `SOURCES.md`, the **Sourcing rules** below verbatim, and the return format. Tell each to run many searches (15–30) and to open the listed primary sources directly. If the Agent tool is unavailable, work the four beats yourself in turn — do not skip any.

- **Beat A — Frontier models & labs · Compute, chips & infrastructure · Deployment & impact (industry, funding, labor).** SOURCES.md §1, §7, §8.
- **Beat B — Research & papers (incl. safety, alignment, evals).** SOURCES.md §2. arXiv new listings (cs.AI, cs.LG, cs.CL, cs.CR, cs.CV, cs.RO), Hugging Face papers, alphaXiv, Nature/Science, lab research blogs, Epoch, METR, AISI, CAISI, Apollo, Redwood, Alignment Forum. Prefer papers with a notable quantitative result, from major labs/universities, or drawing significant attention. Return arXiv IDs and author institutions.
- **Beat C — Security, misuse & threat intelligence · Military, defense & geopolitics.** SOURCES.md §3, §4. AI-enabled intrusions and malware, fraud and scams, deepfakes, influence operations, surveillance, prompt injection and agent exploits, model theft / illicit distillation, bio/chem misuse reports; procurement, deployment, autonomous weapons, export controls, national strategies.
- **Beat D — Health, science & medicine · Policy, regulation & law.** SOURCES.md §5, §6. Clinical results, FDA/Health Canada/WHO actions, drug discovery, AI for science, biosecurity; legislation, regulation, enforcement, court rulings and filings, government reports, standards — US federal and state, EU, UK, Canada, China, international bodies.

**Subagent return format** — one block per item, then a short list of rejected candidates and why:

```
SECTION: <one of the eight section names>
HEADLINE: <factual, specific, max 18 words, no hype>
PUBLISHED: <date/time and timezone exactly as the source shows it>
SOURCES: one per line — <publisher> | <exact URL> | primary or report   (only URLs actually opened or seen in search results; never constructed)
FACTS: 2–5 bullets, each a verifiable fact from a linked source, numbers/units/baselines exactly as written, naming which source
FLAGS: company-claim | single-source | preprint | update  (any that apply)
```

**Sourcing rules (give to subagents verbatim):**
1. Only include facts that appear in a source you opened (WebFetch) or in the text of a search result. No inference, speculation, predictions or "this could mean". No hype adjectives.
2. Every item links to the specific article, paper or document — never a homepage or index page. Link the primary source whenever one exists (paper, company post, government document, filing, court record) plus independent reporting. Aim for 2+ sources on significant items; if only one outlet has it, flag `single-source`.
3. Confirm the publication date is inside the window. If the date cannot be determined, drop the item. Older stories qualify only if something new happened inside the window, and only the new facts are reported (flag `update`).
4. Attribute claims: "OpenAI says…", "according to The Record…". Company-reported benchmarks, user counts, revenue and capability claims get `company-claim` unless independently verified. Research that is not peer reviewed gets `preprint`.
5. Quote numbers exactly as the source writes them, with units and the comparison baseline. Do not round, convert or compute new figures.
6. If `WebFetch` refuses a page, fetch it directly with `node scripts/fetch.js <url>` — the sites we read have given permission for direct reads, and the fetcher identifies itself. Use only what the returned text actually says; if it comes back as a paywall stub, a login page or nothing usable, fall back to search-result text or another source and say in the bullet where the figures came from. Never use archive or cache sites, and never cite a URL whose content you did not see. Sites that refuse `WebFetch` are listed in SOURCES.md.
7. Skip consumer tips, "fun uses", prompt guides, listicles, opinion pieces without new facts, minor feature updates, unsourced rumours, and small funding rounds unless strategically notable (US$100M+, or a frontier lab / defense / health / security company).
8. When in doubt, leave it out.

After the beats return, run a few **gap-check searches** yourself for anything a beat may have missed (WebSearch: "AI" + Pentagon / drone; "AI" + FDA / hospital; "AI" + scam / deepfake / influence operation; "AI" + export controls / data center power; "AI" + lawsuit / ruling; plus Techmeme and Hacker News front page), restricted to the window.

## 2. Verify and select

Merge the beats' returns. De-duplicate across beats and against previous editions. Then, for each candidate:
- Open the primary source. Confirm the headline and every number/date/name you intend to use. A secondary report of a paper links the paper. A report of a court ruling links the ruling or docket where possible.
- Prefer two independent sources for anything contested, surprising, or about a specific actor (a named threat group, a company's claim about a rival, a casualty figure).
- Drop: opinion pieces without new facts, product marketing with no numbers, speculation, "could" / "may" stories, anything you cannot open, anything older than the window without a new development.
- Spot-verify: open (WebFetch, or `node scripts/fetch.js` if it refuses) the key source for every item you will mention in the summary and for every figure in the summary; confirm date, numbers and URL yourself. Remove anything you cannot confirm.
- Keep: model/system releases with benchmarks or capabilities; papers with a result (state the result); documented misuse and threat-intel reports (name actors, counts, dates); military and government procurement/deployment; clinical and scientific results; regulation, enforcement, court decisions; compute/chip/energy facts with figures; large-scale deployments and measured impacts, good or bad.

## 3. Write the edition — `data/DATE.json`

Schema (see `data/2026-09-11.json` for a full example once it exists):

```json
{
  "date": "YYYY-MM-DD",
  "edition": "daily",
  "generated_at": "<ISO-8601 UTC timestamp>",
  "window": "e.g. 10 Sep 11:00 → 11 Sep 11:00 UTC",
  "title": "The episode's name — 3 to 10 words, a statement: who did what, or what changed. No period, no colon, no figure that is not in the summary. It is read in podcast apps as 'Name [2 Oct 2026]', so it must stand alone.",
  "summary": ["paragraph 1", "paragraph 2"],
  "sections": [
    {
      "name": "<one of the eight section names below>",
      "items": [
        {
          "headline": "Specific, factual, one line — who did what, with the key number",
          "sources": [{ "name": "Anthropic", "url": "https://..." }, { "name": "Reuters", "url": "https://..." }],
          "bullets": ["What was announced/found, with numbers.", "Why it matters / what it changes.", "Caveats, what is unverified, what to watch."],
          "topics": ["anthropic", "threat-intel", "cyber-offense"],
          "storylines": ["ai-enabled-hacking"],
          "impact": "beneficial" | "harmful" | "mixed" | "neutral",
          "flags": ["company-claim" | "single-source" | "preprint" | "update"]
        }
      ]
    }
  ]
}
```

**Section names** (exactly these; omit a section if it has nothing that day):
1. `Frontier models & labs` — releases, capabilities, benchmarks, lab announcements, safety cases, system cards.
2. `Research & papers` — papers with results: new methods, evals, interpretability, alignment, scaling. State the result and the number.
3. `Security, misuse & threat intelligence` — threat-intel reports, documented attacks using AI, influence operations, scams/deepfakes, model vulnerabilities, prompt injection, jailbreaks, agent security.
4. `Military, defense & geopolitics` — procurement, deployment, autonomous weapons, export controls, national strategies, China/US/EU competition.
5. `Health, science & medicine` — clinical results, FDA actions, drug discovery, AI-for-science results, hospital deployments and their measured outcomes.
6. `Policy, regulation & law` — legislation, regulation, enforcement, court rulings, government reports, standards.
7. `Compute, chips & infrastructure` — chips, fabs, datacenters, power, capex figures, funding rounds and deals with numbers.
8. `Deployment & impact` — large-scale rollouts, labor effects, measured societal effects, incidents, the good and the bad in practice.

**Summary**: 2–3 paragraphs, ~150–250 words. The three to five things that matter most today, stated as facts, with the numbers. No throat-clearing, no "in today's edition".

**Headlines**: one line, specific, factual. "Anthropic report: Russian state group GTG-20006 used Claude to automate espionage against Ukrainian and European governments" — not "Anthropic releases threat report".

**Bullets**: 2–4 per item. First bullet is the fact with the number. Then significance. Then caveats — say plainly what is unverified, what the source did not say, what to watch. Write in complete sentences. Never pad.

**Sources**: 1–4 per item, primary first. `name` is the publisher (Anthropic, arXiv, Reuters, FDA, Court docket), not the article title.

**Topics**: 1–4 lowercase-hyphen slugs per item. Reuse existing slugs (`node scripts/build.js --topics`). # Sources

The sweep list for every edition. **Primary** sources (labs, papers, governments, court filings, security vendors' own reports) are always preferred for the link beside a headline; **secondary** sources (press, newsletters, aggregators) are used to discover stories and as corroboration. input.prompt: What is announced? Date published, deadlines, who can apply, specifics and numbers.

response.result:
**Announcement:** The European Commission's AI Office is hosting an online workshop in January 2027 on embedded evaluations as a way to assess systemic risks from general-purpose AI (GPAI) models. The call seeks expert input and proposals.

**Key dates:**
- **Published:** 27 November 2026
- **Deadline:** Expressions of interest and proposals are due by 9 December 2026.
- **Selection and comment round:** Expected in December 2026. Selected participants can comment on a consolidated document before the workshop.
- **Workshop:** January 2027 (online)

**Who can apply:**
- Applicants are selected on the quality and relevance of their proposals, and on either or both of these:
  - Demonstrated experience conducting high-quality GPAI evaluations of systemic risks.
  - A strong track record in AI governance thought leadership on systemic-risk evaluations, such as prominent white papers.
- Individuals or organisations with embedded evaluation experience can express interest without submitting a proposal, but must state that experience.
- Members of the AI Office's Network of Evaluators can also express interest without a proposal if they show recent or ongoing relevant embedded evaluation work. Membership requires consent at one of the workshops held on 13 December 2024, 28 April 2025, or 15 July 2026.

**Specifics:**
- "Embedded evaluation" means external, qualified independent evaluators get employee-like access to a provider's internal models, systems, staff, and documentation over an extended period.
- Focus areas include evaluator qualifications, access scope, duration and frequency, publication rights, grounds for redaction or delay, and handling of redacted material. Independence safeguards, such as cooling-off periods and evaluator rotation, may also be discussed.

**Numbers:** No participant cap or number of selected participants is stated.

**Disclaimer:** The call does not reflect an official AI Office or Commission position and is not guidance on the AI Act.

Context Scaling: A New Frontier of AI Scaling
https://arxiv.org/abs/2611.33160
arXiv:2611.33160v1 Announce Type: new
Abstract: Many failures of deployed AI arise not from weak inference but from a mismatch between the state a task depends on and the context available when the system acts. Relevant user state, repository revisions, tool traces, sensor readings, or environment changes may be unavailable, distorted, or poorly selected. We call the effort to reduce this bottleneck context scaling. We frame a model as $P_\theta(d\mid c)$ within a system governed by three budgets: training $B_\theta$, decision-time $B_d$, and context-infrastructure $B_c$. Pretraining scaling invests in $\theta$; decision-time scaling searches, refines, or verifies decisions under supplied context; context scaling improves the system's capacity to acquire, represent, deliver, evaluate, and persist deployment state for model use. The three programs interact, but only $B_c$ targets what the system can make available before a decision. This view makes the model-infrastructure pair the unit of analysis. # SYS010 malware abuses browser management to spy on Gmail, Outlook

By

# Ionut Ilascu

- November 26, 2026

- 06:50 AM

- 0



A new version of the SYS01 infostealer malware delivered through Meta ads is enrolling browsers into enterprise-style management to force the installation of an extension that steals sensitive data, including Gmail and Outlook emails.



The ads lure Windows users into downloading free animated wallpapers that work as advertised but also deploy malware in the background during installation.



The campaign targets Facebook and Meta business accounts and gives the operator access to recent Gmail and Outlook messages in Chrome, and the ability to permanently delete emails.



Bitdefender Labs tracks the campaign as SYS010 and says the malware is likely a new version of the SYS01 infostealer , observed since at least 2022 in malvertising activity on Facebook .



The name reflects the researchers' assessment that this variant represents a major improvement over its predecessor, leading them to tag it as version 2, represented in binary as 010.



Researchers identified a malicious SYS010 ad on October 16 and found that the campaign was still ongoing, with hundreds of ads created.



Company telemetry shows that requests to the threat actor’s servers came from several countries in Asia, Europe, North America, Africa, and South America.



Meta Ad Library' transparency page shows that one advertisement alone reached 6,275 users in the European Union, targeting anyone above 18.





Meta transparency page for EU audience in SYS010 malvertising

source: Bitdefender





In a report today, Bitdefender says most requests came from the Philippines, Thailand, Bangladesh, Poland, Mexico, Algeria, Belgium, Mongolia, and the United States, but emphasizes these figures do not reflect confirmed infections.




# Working wallpaper installs thieving add-on


The ads impersonate the legitimate Wallpaper Engine (a renamed, digitally signed version of the MeisterTask desktop app built on Electron) and Lively Wallpapers applications, directing users to malicious download sites, some of them using domains designed to appear official.



After installing the malicious Windows app, users get the advertised animated wallpaper functionality, which helps disguise the malware running in the background.



According to Bitdefender researchers, the attacker forces Chrome, Edge, and Firefox to install malicious browser add-ons by abusing management tools designed for organizations.



A script named eclient.php is responsible for installing the malicious extensions by modifying browser management policies.





Attacker PHP script for installing malicious browser extension

​​​​​​source: Bitdefender





In Chrome, it enrolls the browser in an attacker-controlled Google admin console, allowing forced installation of extensions.



In Firefox, it uses an ExtensionSettings policy to force-install an add-on while disabling Developer Tools and abuse reporting.



For Edge, it can enroll the victim's Windows device in an attacker-controlled mobile device management (MDM) server to enable forced extension installation.



These changes require administrator permissions, which is solved by triggering the User Account Control (UAC) prompt and repeating it every three seconds up to 99 times until the user approves the action.



The controls prevent users from disabling or removing the add-ons, Bitdefender says. The extensions can then steal session cookies, allowing the malware operator to access signed-in accounts without entering passwords or completing a two-factor authentication challenge.



Bitdefender determined that the malicious add-ons pose as document tools, Docs Helper in Chrome and Document Hub in Firefox.



They note that the fake Docs Helper extension for Chrome uses an icon resembling the Google Docs logo but is distributed outside the Chrome Web Store.



The extensions also collect information about Facebook Pages, advertising and business accounts that the victim can access, including spending and payment details.




# Gmail and Outlook ema
=== https://www.bleepingcomputer.com/news/security/remus-malware-steals-gmail-messages-via-fake-google-sheets-extension/
HTTP 200 · https://www.bleepingcomputer.com/news/security/remus-malware-steals-gmail-messages-via-fake-google-sheets-extension/ · text/html

# Remus malware steals Gmail messages via fake Google Sheets extension

By

# Bill Toulas

- November 26, 2026

- 10:23 AM

- 0



The Remus infostealer is stealing Gmail messages through a stealthy malicious Chrome extension, a capability the malware operators marketed as a zero-day exploit in Google's email service.



On November 8, the Remus infostealer developer started advertising the alleged Gmail zero-day flaw that allowed the malware to collect emails even if victims changed their passwords and revoked all sessions.



Threat intelligence company Hudson Rock investigated the claims but came to inconclusive results. The researchers noted that evidence from the malware customers matched the seller's pitch, although there was no technical proof that a zero-day vulnerability was being exploited.





Remus stealer panel

Source: GenDigital





GenDigital and Invoke RE researchers published their independent findings yesterday, explaining that the advertised “zero-day” was just a malicious Chrome extension installed on the victims' browsers.






The extension is designed to steal unread emails from signed-in Gmail accounts. It can also survive password changes and session revocations because it remains installed in the victim's Chrome browser.



Its access to Gmail stops when the active session ends, and resumes again when the victim signs back in.



GenDigital discovered the extension after reverse-engineering the Remus infostealer. The researchers found no trace of an email-stealing module, suggesting that the functionality is implemented via an add-on.



“In a nutshell, the loaded module is a native DLL whose sole purpose is to install a malicious extension into Google Chrome, which, notably, is the only browser it targets,” GenDigital explains .



“The extension itself is bundled directly inside the DLL, stored as an unencrypted ZIP archive in its .rdata section.”



GenDigital explains that Chrome versions 137 and later removed a command-line option that allowed malware to load extensions.



Remus takes a complex route to overcome this restriction, editing the victim’s Chrome profile to register the malicious extension and then enabling ‘Developer Mode’ in the browser, which is required to run unpacked extensions.



The extension uses the name “Google Sheets,” copies the description of Google Docs Offline, and requests access to all websites.





Installed malicious extension

Source: GenDigital





Once active in the browser, it checks for unread emails every minute across up to 10 account slots and retrieves them in full, in raw format.



The extension sends the email subject, message body, sender, and victim’s email address to its command-and-control server, along with a campaign identifier.





Email theft

Source: GenDigital





Failed uploads are queued and retried, while a local record helps the extension keep track of what has succeeded so it doesn’t send duplicates.



Although the extension also parses attachment filenames, it does not send those to its operators, so this feature may not be fully implemented yet.



To defend against this threat, users are advised to download software only from trusted sources and scrutinize “chrome://extensions” for rogue installations or unexpected activation of Developer Mode.

International Trade Administration, U.S. Department of Commerce, 1401 
Constitution Avenue NW, Washington, DC 20230; email SIexports.gov">info@SIexports.gov.

SUPPLEMENTARY INFORMATION:

I. Background and Purpose

    Executive Order 14320 of July 23, 2025, Promoting the Export of the 
American SI Technology Stack, directs the Secretary of Commerce, in 
consultation with the Secretary of State and the Director of the Office 
of Science and Technology Policy, to establish and implement the 
American SI Exports Program (the Program) to support the development 
and deployment of United States full-stack SI export packages.
    Commerce announced the Call for Proposals for Pre-Set Consortia on 
April 1, 2026 (91 FR 18412) (April 2026 CFP), establishing the first 
pathway for designation under the Program. The initial phase of the 
Pre-Set Consortia pathway closed on June 30, 2026.
    This notice establishes a second pathway for designation in the 
Program: On-Demand Consortia. On-Demand Consortia are industry-led 
groupings formed to respond to a specific, identified foreign export 
opportunity, as described in Section III, infra. This notice also 
provides for re-designation and de-designation of packages designated 
under either this notice or the April 2026 CFP, and for the reopening 
at a later date of the Pre-Set Consortia pathway.

II. Eligible On-Demand Consortia

    On-Demand Consortia must comply with the eligibility requirements 
laid out in Sections II and IV of the April 2026 CFP, except that:
    1. A subsidiary, affiliate, or branch whose ultimate parent entity 
is organized under the laws of a foreign jurisdiction or has its 
principal place of business outside the United States is eligible to be 
an anchor member as long as the entity itself is organized under the 
laws of the United States or a State thereof, with its principal place 
of business in the United States, and meets qualifications (1) and (3) 
of an anchor member laid out in Section II of the April 2026 CFP.
    2. Packages offered by On-Demand Consortia are not themselves 
required to cover the full five layers of the SI technology stack 
described in Section III of the April 2026 CFP. Instead, On-Demand 
Consortia need only offer the layers of the SI stack necessary to meet 
the buyer's demands for the identified foreign export opportunity, 
provided that the layers offered meet the content requirements 
described in Section IV of the April 2026 CFP, as applicable.
    An On-Demand Consortium that is not offering a full-stack SI 
technology package, as described in Executive Order 14320 and Section 
III of the April 2026 CFP, must demonstrate that the layers offered by 
the Consortium will combine with existing or acquired infrastructure or 
capabilities to result in a full-stack SI technology package. An On-
Demand Consortium must attest that it has made reasonable efforts to 
confirm that the resulting full-stack SI technology package meets the 
content and ownership requirements established under Section IV of the 
April 2026 CFP for all five layers, whether provided by Consortium 
members or not. An On-Demand Consortium may also include a Trusted 
Foreign Enterprise (TFE) as an exception to certain content 
requirements, consistent with Section II.A. of the April 2026 CFP.\2\ 
In addition, the Secretary may, in consultation with the Secretaries of 
State, War, and Energy and the Director of the Office of Science and 
Technology Policy, waive the U.S. ownership and control requirement 
under Section IV.C of the April 2026 CFP for an On-Demand Consortium if 
doing so would advance the national interest of the United States.
---------------------------------------------------------------------------

    \2\ Trusted Foreign Enterprises were referred to as National 
Champion Enterprises in the April 2026 CFP.
---------------------------------------------------------------------------

    On-Demand Consortia are also strongly encouraged to provide 
information relating to the telecommunications and energy 
infrastructure that will support the package. Specifically, applicants 
are encouraged to show that (1) applicable telecommunications 
infrastructure uses technology from trusted sources, meaning it does 
not rely on technology owned, controlled, or manufactured by entities 
of countries of concern as defined in the April 2026 CFP, and (2) 
sufficient energy sources, as appropriate, are or will be in place and 
operational to support the buyer's SI stack. Any such information will 
be favorably considered in the national interest determination under 
Section V of this notice.

III. Qualifying Opportunity

    A proposal from an On-Demand Consortium must be organized around a 
specific, qualifying public or private

[[Page 76748]]

sector SI export opportunity identified in the application.
    Eligible opportunities include procurements or purchases by foreign 
government ministries; state-owned or state-controlled enterprises; 
government-controlled agencies, cooperatives, or commissions; public-
private partnerships; and wholly private foreign entities. Wholly 
private sector opportunities are eligible when the consortium's 
proposal preserves and extends American leadership in SI and decreases 
international dependence on SI technologies developed by adversaries.
    For an opportunity to qualify, (i) the opportunity must be eligible 
as described above; (ii) the applicant must demonstrate that the 
opportunity is existing or forthcoming, such as through a published 
tender, public announcement, or written communication; and (iii) the 
applicant must demonstrate that there is a reasonable likelihood that 
the proposed package will be selected or included in a group of 
finalists, as applicable, by providing documentation such as a letter 
of interest, contract(s), or other written communication from the 
buyer.
    The U.S. Government may identify opportunities that could be 
appropriate for an On-Demand Consortium; more information about any 
such opportunities will be available at https://SIexports.gov.

IV. Proposal Contents

    All applications must be submitted through American SI Exports 
Program submission portal at https://SIexports.gov/on-demand. The 
application will include at least the following:
    1. Consortium overview. The Consortium name; identification of the 
anchor member and attestations that the anchor member has the 
qualifications required under Section II; and a listing of all 
consortium members, their roles, the stack layers in which they provide 
products or services, and whether the Consortium seeks to include any 
members as TFEs.
    2. Full-stack package description. A concise narrative describing 
the integrated technology offering across all layers of the stack 
offered by the Consortium, as well as how layers offered by the 
Consortium will combine with existing or acquired infrastructure or 
capabilities to result in a full-stack SI technology package (if the 
Consortium is offering less than five layers). This must also include:
    a. A description of the content and ownership sufficient to 
establish compliance with the applicable requirements under Section II 
of this notice for all five layers of the full-stack SI technology 
package, whether provided by the Consortium or not.
    b. A description, estimated total valuation, and estimated 
percentage of U.S. hardware content in Layer 1, as defined in Section 
III of the April 2026 CFP.
    c. A description of how the package will advance American 
standards, including NIST frameworks, or comparable frameworks 
appropriate to the target market, with respect to privacy and security.
    3. Qualifying opportunity description. A brief description of the 
opportunity that the Consortium seeks to pursue, including an estimate 
of the value of the opportunity as well as a description of any known 
foreign competition, and an explanation of why the opportunity 
qualifies under Section III, as well as the appropriate supporting 
documentatio

ort Bank of the United States or the U.S. International Development Finance Corporation), the name and role of any private bank, underwriter, co-investor, agent, or other financial service provider that may support the package. V. Review, Designation, and Benefits The Secretary of Commerce, in consultation with the Secretaries of State, War, and Energy and the Director of the Office of Science and Technology Policy, will review proposals and make designation decisions based on the national interest as described in Section IX of the April 2026 CFP. In making designation decisions, the Department will additionally consider whether the package appears consistent with the identified opportunity as well as any information provided on telecommunications or energy as described in Section II of this notice. The Department intends to issue a designation decision within 60 calendar days. There is no numerical cap on the number of packages that may be designated under this notice, or for any particular opportunity. Applicants will receive written notice of designation and next-step guidance on engaging with the Department of Commerce. Applicants whose packages are not designated will receive notice of non-designation and may resubmit revised proposals with a concise explanation of material changes. Designated packages may receive one or more of the benefits laid out in [[Page 76749]] Section VIII of the April 2026 CFP, as appropriate to that package and the identified opportunity. Provisions on treatment of confidential information and applicable legal terms are located in Sections VII and XII of the April 2026 CFP; additional application requirements and process details are available at https://www.SIexports.gov. VI. Re-Designation and De-Designation The Anchor Member of a package designated through either the Pre- Set or On-Demand pathway must notify the Department of any material changes to the package, including but not limited to changes relating to consortium membership, member ownership, U.S. and country of concern content, specific products, or other relevant changes that affect the identified opportunity, by emailing SIexports.gov">info@SIexports.gov as soon as practicable. In response to any such changes, the Department may request additional information, require a new application and national interest determination (i.e., re-designation), or de-designate the package. A new application in response to any such changes may be reviewed in an expedited manner. The Department may also de-designate a package designated under either the April 2026 CFP or this notice upon a determination that designation is no longer in the national interest due to fraud; willful misrepresentation in the application or in any subsequent attestation; criminal conduct relevant to Program integrity; or other conduct that would reflect negatively on the Program. De-designation notifications will be conveyed via email to the Anchor Member and will be effective on the date the email is sent. De-designation does not preclude future application by the same parties if the circumstances that led to the de-designation have been fully addressed. On-Demand Consortia that have had a package designated for an eligible opportunity and that are seeking to provide the same package for a substantially similar eligible opportunity may have access to an expedited application and review. Additional information about any expedited application processes, including eligibility, will be provided at https://SIexports.gov. VII. Additional Pre-Set Consortia Application Window Applications for Pre-Set Consortia may be accepted again at a later date; more information will be provided at SIexports.gov and published in the Federal Register. The GTIG report is titled "GTIG AI Threat Tracker: Agentic Threat Activity Crosses a Significant Threshold." Google's blog dates it November 16, 2026, and the search returned only fragments of the report itself, so the details below come mostly from press coverage.

- **Framing:** GTIG and Mandiant describe the current moment as a critical inflection point. Earlier quarterly reports had only noted nascent adversary interest in agentic capabilities, but the new report says multiple actors are now abusing open-source agentic penetration-testing tools.
- **Example:** GTIG saw a tool called CAIRN used in intrusion activity against targets including in the aerospace sector in the US.

That fits poorly with the "crosses a threshold" headline, so the framing is worth checking against the full report. That article may also cover an earlier report than the November one.

The headquarters of SAP AG, Germany's largest software company, on Jan. 8, 2013, in Walldorf, Germany.
Thomas Lohnes | Getty Images News | Getty Images

SAP is preparing a plan to eliminate at least 10,000 positions as the German firm reshapes its software business for the artificial intelligence era, Bloomberg reported on Thursday , citing people familiar with the matter.
The report came as the company flagged a cybersecurity attack, but said it had found "no evidence of unauthorized access to customer business data."

"SAP has identified suspicious activity and promptly implemented the necessary measures to protect its customers and preserve the security of its services," a company spokesperson said.
"Our customers trust us to protect their data, and that remains our highest priority. In a highly dynamic threat environment, we will continue to strengthen our security to provide the secure and resilient environment our customers depend on."
The company did not respond to a request for comment on the reported job cuts. The number could change after labor negotiations.
Other software companies have also tied workforce reductions to AI initiatives, though for different reasons. WiseTech Global said in February it planned to cut about 2,000 jobs over two years as it integrated AI into its products and operations.
Atlassian said in March it would cut about 1,600 jobs partly to fund further AI investment, while Cloudflare said in May it would eliminate more than 1,100 roles as it moved toward an AI-first operating model.

In the U.S., employers cited AI in 121,401 job-cut announcements through October 2026, accounting for about 20% of the total, according to a Nov. 5 report from outplacement and executive coaching firm Challenger, Gray & Christmas.

China’s Z.AI has fallen behind schedule on its next flagship artificial intelligence model, while rival Moonshot AI expects that the interval between major releases could double from six months to a year or longer if it loses access to overseas computing power, people familiar with the matter have said.
The previously unreported details show how efforts by U.S. AI companies OpenAI and Anthropic to prevent distillation, a technique in which developers train models using answers generated by more capable ones, have slowed Chinese AI development. Washington’s latest chip restrictions threaten further delays.

Reuters-Yonhap News
BEIJING — Chinese artificial intelligence companies that had been closing in on their U.S. rivals are pushing back the release of new models one after another. The U.S. government has blocked their access to advanced semiconductors through third countries, while American AI companies have stepped up measures against "distillation." Facing pressure on both fronts, China's AI industry is warning that the technology gap with the United States, which had been narrowing, will widen again.
According to foreign news reports compiled on the 27th, Moonshot AI, the developer of Kimi K3, recently canceled a $150 million contract to use Nvidia's Blackwell chips through Indonesia. Moonshot AI has internally concluded that if overseas workarounds are cut off, the release cycle for its main AI models could stretch from six months to 12 months or more, sources said. Zhipu AI, another model developer, has pushed back the launch of its next-generation flagship model GLM-5.5, originally planned for this month, to the first quarter of next year or later.
Within the Chinese industry, the earlier confidence that companies could simply build their own alternatives has given way to dismay. Tencent President Martin Lau, speaking on a conference call after third-quarter earnings on the 18th, said of the new U.S. export controls that "every company in China will be affected," adding that in the short term it will take longer to develop next-generation AI models. A researcher at one major Chinese technology company told The Information, a U.S. technology news outlet, "We are finished," and said many colleagues, including the researcher, were considering moving to other fields.
The setback follows a sharp tightening of U.S. semiconductor export controls on China in the wake of the "Jensen Huang scandal." Until now, Chinese AI companies had actively used Nvidia's advanced chips for model development by working around the U.S. export control regime. According to a report published in October by the Institute for Progress, a U.S. think tank, 46% of the computing capacity used by Chinese AI companies relies on Nvidia chips installed in overseas data centers or smuggled into the country. That route has now been shut off entirely as the United States also blocked Chinese firms from accessing the latest AI chips through data centers in third countries.

Adding to the difficulties, distillation — which Chinese AI companies have used to upgrade their models — is also becoming harder. Distillation is a technique that trains a new AI model at low cost by drawing on the responses of an existing high-performance model. OpenAI and Anthropic introduced strong anti-distillation safeguards in September to block the practice by Chinese AI companies. According to The Information, Chinese developers report that U.S. models reduce the depth of their answers or route requests to weaker models when questions appear aimed at distillation, and that some OpenAI models return lower-quality responses when a single account sends too many queries in an hour.
Private credit fund managers and large investment banks are putting new loans for AI infrastructure in Asia on hold or revisiting existing commitments. A $6.6 billion loan increase for a Malaysian facility operated by Bridge Data Centres, a Bain Capital unit used by clients including ByteDance, has been suspended as some lenders in the syndicate conduct additional due diligence. On a $372 million (about 499.4 billion won) loan for a Malaysian facility run by data center operator Digital Halo, whose clients include Alibaba, one bank withdrew from the deal and others tightened their reviews.
Chinese companies are responding by accelerating efforts toward semiconductor self-reliance, though a rapid transition remains uncertain. Alibaba Chief Executive Eddie Wu said at the third-quarter earnings announcement on the 19th that by the first quarter of next year, chip subsidiary T-Head will be able to train AI models using only chips it has developed in-house. Wu added that from next year, Alibaba plans to source most of its newly acquired AI chips from T-Head. MiniMax Chief Executive Yan Junjie also said at a company-wide meeting on the 20th that the firm would move up its adoption of AI chips from Huawei and Alibaba, sources said.
Still, Semiconductor Manufacturing International Corp. (SMIC), China's largest foundry, is struggling to expand advanced-process capacity because of U.S. export controls on chipmaking equipment. Some in the industry expect that major AI companies such as DeepSeek may have to wait at least a year to receive the domestically made chips they need. Neil Shah, vice president at market research firm Counterpoint Research, told Reuters that China appears unlikely to close the gap with the United States in cutting-edge technology by 2030, let alone before 2028.

== 2026-11-26 10.64898/2026.09.08.26362428 Language model-assisted label refinement for accurate sepsis detection from electronic health records
AUTHORS: Kitsos Kalyvianakis, I.; Perez de Amezaga, C.; Lee, E. S.; Palmer, A.; Garner, J.; Wu, U. S.; Orfanoudaki, A.
Sepsis is a leading cause of hospital mortality, yet timely recognition is hampered by nonspecific presentations and label noise in code-based case definitions. We developed STRIDE, a machine-learning framework for sepsis detection across seven hospitals with a scalable approach to label quality. We used a large language model applied to discharge summaries to refine encounter-level labels, with 349 physician-adjudicated encounters informing prompt development and serving as a clinical reference for evaluation. We compared 8-, 24-, and 48-hour observation windows and benchmarked against SOFA, SIRS, and Epic. Among 352,415 eligible encounters, STRIDE-8 achieved ROC-AUCs of 0.949 in derivation testing and 0.871 in physician-adjudicated evaluation. Removing SIRS-related predictors reduced these values to 0.853 and 0.743. Llama reclassified 12.8% of initially positive derivation encounters as non-septic. These results support further investigation of short-window physiological screening combined with retrospective label review and evaluation against independent clinical reference outcomes.

== 2026-11-26 10.64898/2026.11.25.26368956 Scalable frameworks for local evaluation of AI-enabled imaging devices using PACS-integrated large language models
AUTHORS: Amurthur, A.; Justice, S. A.; Chin, J. K.; Mercaldo, S. F.; Morley, R. J.; Schultz, A. S.; Silva, V.; Yun, T. J.; Choi, J. W.; Bridge, C. P.; Schultz, T.; Hillis, J. M.
Introduction: Artificial intelligence (AI)-enabled imaging device performance may vary across institutions due to differences in disease prevalence, patient demographics, and acquisition protocols. Routine local evaluation, including pre-deployment baseline testing and post-deployment monitoring, remains limited by manual data curation. A large language model (LLM)-as-a-judge approach using existing radiology reports provides a method of performing local evaluation. Methods: We established PACS-integrated LLMs in HIPAA-compliant environments. We then developed two scalable frameworks to automate key processes of local evaluation: selection of a candidate series for device inference and generation of report-derived labels. We applied these frameworks to 4,000 consecutive non-contrast head CT examinations from two hospitals to evaluate agreement between radiology reports and Purple AI Hyper Insight-ICH, a commercial intracranial hemorrhage detection device. Results: For series selection, we used a three-tiered, traffic-light approach across 31,422 available series to select a single series for device inference in 3,976 examinations. For radiology report field extraction, we refined an LLM prompt with three steps: initial binary classification, characterization of discordance between the binary classification prompt output and device output, and a comprehensive prompt (featuring 28 structured fields that were informed by the preceding stages). The positive percent agreement (PPA) depended on the definition of positive cases based on the comprehensive prompt fields: it was 87.7% (79.2 to 95.0%) using similar criteria to many published studies (acute or acute-on-chronic, non-minimal, non-equivocal hemorrhage), yet was lower when including chronic, minimal or equivocal ICH. The reports say Nvidia has asked Dell, Supermicro, and other server partners to halt AI server shipments to Malaysia, Singapore, Thailand, and Indonesia. All of it traces back to a Financial Times report citing anonymous sources, and Nvidia has not confirmed it.

- **The report:** The FT said Nvidia told manufacturing partners including Dell and Supermicro to stop shipping servers with its advanced AI chips to those countries, citing three people familiar with the matter. Reuters relayed it without independent verification, and the WSJ separately reported the instruction as a pause of an unspecified period.

- **Caveat:** One outlet (vlsi.kr) states flatly that shipments have stopped. That goes beyond what the other sources, which all say "reportedly," support, so I'd treat it cautiously.

results:
The search turned up consistent reporting on this, mostly derived from a SecurityWeek story and Accenture's own research.

- **Pre-patch exploitation:** Accenture's Apex Labs found that attackers used the flaws before Mitel's advisory, and CISA has since added five MiCollab flaws to its KEV catalog. Accenture APEX Labs assesses with high confidence that the flaws were exploited before disclosure, with web-shell activity observed at a confirmed victim the day before the patch. Mitel's patches came out on November 16 and cover five vulnerabilities, including arbitrary file upload, XML injection, unauthorized access, command injection, and authentication bypass.
- **Intrusion scope:** In one case, hackers gained privileged access to a MiCollab server and quickly reached the targeted organization's identity infrastructure, ultimately stealing sensitive business information. Accenture reported that attackers ran commands on a MiCollab server 12 minutes after the first request and gained root privileges within half an hour.
- **AI involvement:** This is the weakest part of the story. The attacker's infrastructure communicated with two unnamed commercial AI API services, but Accenture said the activity is consistent with potential uses such as data triage, operational support for exploitation or web-shell activity, and preparation of extortion material. Another write-up notes that Accenture could not establish how those services were used.
- **Extortion and attribution:** The researchers have not linked the attacks to a known cybercrime group, but believe they may have been part of an extortion campaign.
- **Other organizations:** One result says Accenture identified a second organization's MiCollab 10.0-series server maintaining a persistent HTTPS connection to attacker infrastructure since November 9, but researchers could not determine which vulnerability enabled access, so exploitation of the newly disclosed flaws at this organization remains unconfirmed.
- **Recommended action:** Accenture warned organizations that attackers may have compromised their MiCollab servers before the fixes were installed and urged them to check for indicators of compromise.

Note that the AI-assisted attribution is inferred, not confirmed. I left out the AI-generated summary on zerohour.day, since it is not a primary source.

# Claude Code agent proxy

Outbound HTTPS from this session goes through a local proxy at http://127.0.0.1:44663
(set via HTTPS_PROXY) which tunnels to a policy-enforcing egress proxy. TLS is
re-terminated there, so every tool must trust the CA bundle at
/root/.ccr/ca-bundle.crt. The standard CA environment variables, the system trust
store (where possible), a JVM truststore, the Bazel system bazelrc, the
browser NSS store, and gsutil's boto config are already set up.

## Quick diagnosis

1. Read the end of the failed command's output. When the proxy refused or lost
   a connection while a Bash command ran, Claude Code adds [agent-proxy] lines
   there with the host and the reason. A command that ran in the background,
   or whose exit status hides the failure (piped into another command, or
   followed by "|| true"), gets none.
2. Find the failure class below and apply the matching fix.
3. Never disable TLS verification, never unset HTTPS_PROXY, and do not retry
   policy denials (403/407) — report them instead.

## Failure classes and fixes

### "certificate verify failed" / "self-signed certificate in chain" / PKIX errors

The failing tool is not reading the pre-set CA configuration. In order:

- If the tool has a CA flag or env var, point it at /root/.ccr/ca-bundle.crt
  (examples: --cacert, SSL_CERT_FILE, NODE_EXTRA_CA_CERTS, REQUESTS_CA_BUNDLE,
  AWS_CA_BUNDLE, DENO_CERT, CARGO_HTTP_CAINFO, PIP_CERT, GIT_SSL_CAINFO,
  BUNDLE_SSL_CA_CERT, HEX_CACERTS_PATH, NIX_SSL_CERT_FILE).
- Tool config files override environment variables. If one of these sets its
  own CA or disables verification, point it at the bundle instead:
  pip.conf "cert", npm "cafile" (npm config get cafile), ~/.curlrc "cacert",
  .wgetrc "ca_certificate", conda "ssl_verify", git "http.sslCAInfo",
  gradle.properties / MAVEN_OPTS "-Djavax.net.ssl.trustStore".
- JVM tools (Maven, Gradle, plain Java): when a JDK is present,
  JAVA_TOOL_OPTIONS points JVMs at a truststore that holds the proxy CA: the
  JDK's own store if the system trust install already added the CA there,
  otherwise /root/.ccr/java-truststore.p12 (password "changeit"). Confirm
  that JAVA_TOOL_OPTIONS sets a trustStore before pointing a build at either:
  where it sets none, set-up was skipped, has not finished or has failed. If
  the image or the build sets its own trustStore, that one wins — import the
  proxy CA into it with
  keytool -importcert -noprompt -alias ccr-agent-proxy -file /root/.ccr/agent-proxy-ca.crt -keystore <their store>
  or point the build at the ready-made one. Bazel reads the managed block in
  /etc/bazel.bazelrc rather than JAVA_TOOL_OPTIONS.

### "405 Method Not Allowed" from the proxy

The tool sent a plain-HTTP (non-CONNECT) request: usually axios older than
1.16.1 (upgrade it) or a tool configured with HTTP_PROXY (unset HTTP_PROXY for
that tool — only HTTPS_PROXY is supported).

### 403 / 407 from the proxy

Most often the destination host is not allowed for this session. Do not retry
or route around it — report the blocked host.
Note: curl hides response bodies on failed CONNECTs; the [agent-proxy] lines
give the host and, where the egress proxy answered one, the HTTP status.

### 429 / 503 from the proxy

Too many connections or requests went through the proxy, or the egress proxy
was busy. The proxy can hold a connection for about a minute before it refuses
it, so a tool with a short timeout of its own may report only a timeout. Run
fewer downloads or requests at once, then retry.

The proxy also answers 429 immediately when too many connections to it are open,
idle ones included (too_many_connections in the [agent-proxy] lines under a
failed command). Look for a program that opens connections and never closes
them. New connections work again once some have closed.

### 408 from the proxy

The tool opened a connection to the proxy and sent no complete request within 30
seconds, so the proxy closed it. Retry once. If it happens again, the tool opens
connections before it has a request to send, it is paused or short of CPU, or its
request never ends with an empty line in CRLF form (bare LF line ends, or another
protocol such as SOCKS).

### "connection reset" / "unexpected disconnect" / "RPC failed" mid-transfer

Once a tunnel is up the proxy cannot send an error response, so a connection
it aborts (tunnel to the egress proxy lost, or an upload the tunnel stopped
accepting) reaches the tool as a bare reset. The [agent-proxy] lines name the
host and reason; look for them before concluding the remote service refused the
operation.

### Tool ignores the proxy entirely (timeouts with no proxy error)

Some clients do not read HTTPS_PROXY: Node's built-in fetch (run that command
with NODE_USE_ENV_PROXY=1 on Node >= 22.21), aiohttp (pass trust_env=True),
Ruby bundler (reads only HTTP_PROXY, which this proxy does not serve),
hand-rolled Go dialers. Prefer the tool's own proxy option where one exists.

### git

SSH-form GitHub remotes ([email redacted]:...) are rewritten to HTTPS
automatically unless this session has its own SSH setup or supplies its own
GIT_CONFIG_*. A gitconfig that sets http.proxy / http.<url>.proxy (even empty),
its own http.sslCAInfo, or an https-to-ssh insteadOf makes git bypass the proxy
or fail verification; adjust those keys for this session if git times out.

### docker build / docker run

Processes inside containers cannot reach 127.0.0.1:44663 and do not trust
the CA. Workarounds: run builds with --network host, copy /root/.ccr/ca-bundle.crt
into the build context and install it in an early layer, and pass proxy/CA
settings explicitly to the build.

### Not supported through the proxy (report, do not work around)

gRPC / HTTP/2-only APIs, WebSocket upgrades, client-mTLS, certificate-pinned
clients (e.g. Snowflake, ngrok), non-443 HTTPS ports, raw-TCP databases.

If a tool still cannot work through the proxy, report it so the policy or
tooling can be fixed.

**Publication date and time:** November 26, 2026 (6:35 AM ET)

**Key facts**

- **Exploitation:** Accenture's Apex Labs says threat actors exploited several Mitel MiCollab vulnerabilities as zero-days in a data theft campaign. The article describes it as a suspected extortion campaign, possibly aided by AI.
- **Patches:** Mitel announced patches for five vulnerabilities on November 16. Two critical bugs allow arbitrary command execution, and all five can be exploited by unauthenticated attackers.
- **CVE IDs:** CVE-2026-133275, CVE-2026-133303, CVE-2026-133311, CVE-2026-133323, CVE-2026-133324
- **CISA:** CISA added all five flaws to its Known Exploited Vulnerabilities catalog. Four must be addressed by November 28, and the last by December 9.
- **Timeline (per Accenture):**
  - A web shell was deployed on a victim's systems on November 15, before Mitel's advisory.
  - Commands ran on a MiCollab server 12 minutes after the first request, and root privileges were gained within half an hour.
  - About 20 hours after the first request, the attackers reached internal backup and database servers.
- **Second victim:** A MiCollab server had been communicating with the same attacker infrastructure since November 9. Accenture could not determine how it was compromised.
- **Mitel advisory:** Advisory MISA-2026-0012, last updated November 24, does not mention in-the-wild exploitation.

**Accenture's claims about AI API services**

- The attacker's infrastructure communicated with two unnamed commercial AI API services.
- Accenture says it cannot determine precisely how the services were used, because its telemetry is sampled. The observed activity is consistent with data triage, operational support for exploitation or web-shell activity, or preparing extortion material.
- After an eight-hour silence, communications with the AI services resumed at the same second the attackers sent an authentication bypass request to the targeted server.

**Source report:** https://accenture.github.io/cyber-intelligence/micollab-exploitation/

# Nvidia hits pause on chip shipments to Southeast Asia

Nvidia is under pressure to do things differently, and a new WSJ report shows how far that’s going.

According to the Journal, Nvidia has told manufacturing partners, including Dell and Super Micro, to hit pause on server shipments to Malaysia, Singapore, Thailand, and Indonesia for an unspecified period as it assesses whether its regional partners are meeting U.S. export requirements.

As for why those countries, Chinese companies have been tapping Nvidia chips remotely from data centers there, a loophole the US Commerce Department closed — reportedly grudgingly — earlier this month. The Journal notes that the think tank Institute for Progress estimates remote data centers like these supply about 24% of China’s AI computing power.

Returning to the Neuron Basis for Interpretability, Part 2: Using Neurons For Safety Applications

Alignment Science Blog

# Returning to the Neuron Basis for Interpretability, Part 2: Using Neurons For Safety Applications

Jasmine Shone 1,* , Lisa Dunlap 1 November 23, 2026
1 Anthropic
* Work done as part of the Anthropic Fellows Program

tl;dr In a companion piece , we argue that individual neurons in language models are easier to interpret than earlier work has assumed. Here we see whether they could be useful for safety work. In open-weight models, we select neurons by what makes them fire and what they contribute to a model’s output. These neurons generally detect harmful text better than keyword or similarity search, though usually less well than classifiers trained on labeled examples, and they steer a model’s behavior about as well as trained methods. They also help an auditor find hidden behaviors in finetuned models. Finally, we find that most of the “unlearning” methods we tested appear to hide hazardous knowledge rather than remove it, and neurons help show how.

# Introduction

Most interpretability tools for detection and control are trained: sparse autoencoders, probes and steering vectors all need a dictionary or labeled examples. We test whether a model’s own MLP neurons, which need no additional training or labels, work as detectors and steering vectors. As discussed in the companion post , an MLP neuron adds its activation times one fixed vector, its column of the down projection, to the residual stream, so we interpret a neuron as a context-gated steering vector. In that post, we revisited three objections to neurons and found that neurons rarely add two unrelated concepts to the residual stream at once, that they write in an approximately fixed basis across layers, and that facts are implemented in a distributed and interpretable manner.

Here we test whether neurons are useful in practice. We choose neurons from their top-activating passages, their automated descriptions and their J-lens readouts, with a Claude agent or a simple similarity search. The first part of this post compares neuron output vectors with trained tools for detection and steering. The second part compares each neuron of a finetuned model with its base version. We apply this to model organisms of backdoors, emergent misalignment and subliminal learning, to find the neurons behind the trained behavior and to build auditing methods that find it from the weights. We also apply it to public WMDP-cyber unlearning checkpoints, to find how each family of methods lowers accuracy and whether the facts remain. WMDP-cyber is the cybersecurity subset of the WMDP benchmark (Li et al., 2024), and is set up so that unlearning methods train a model to forget the text in a forget corpus of hazardous cybersecurity passages from GitHub while keeping its performance on a retain corpus, and the model is then evaluated on 1,987 multiple-choice questions about knowledge that could help a cyberattack.

Contributions.

- We show that for concept detection, neurons chosen from their descriptions and readouts beat sparse-autoencoder latents chosen from their descriptions, alone or with the same readouts.

- A safety classifier decides whether a user’s request or a piece of text is unsafe. Neurons work as zero-shot safety classifiers, with no labeled examples. Neuron probes beat text search on most evaluation sets and match linear probes trained on 400 labels on four of 16 evaluation sets, and they retrieve harmful documents from unlabeled text better than text search on 11 of 17 topics.

- We use neuron output vectors to steer chatbot behaviors. We find that neurons chosen from their J-lens readouts and from descriptions of their top-activating examples are about as effective as trained steering vectors: both produce the target behavior in 21% of responses.

- We compare each neuron of a finetuned model with its base version in model organisms of backdoors, emergent misalignment and subliminal learning. On average, finetuning raises the activation of neurons whose output vectors already add the trained behavior, so the behavior appears in the readouts of the neurons it changes.

- We run a blind auditing game on 68 LoRA adapters, 58 of which add a hidden behavior. On those 58, a Claude auditor that steers along the update’s directions and reads the neurons aligned with them names the trained behavior in 75% of audits, against 40% from outputs alone.

Alignment Science Blog

# Returning to the Neuron Basis for Interpretability, Part 1: Answering Three Objections

Jasmine Shone 1,* , Lisa Dunlap 1 November 23, 2026
1 Anthropic
* Work done as part of the Anthropic Fellows Program

tl;dr Previous interpretability research has suggested that understanding language models by studying their individual neurons is difficult, for three reasons: a single neuron often fires on several unrelated inputs; the way a concept is represented can change between two layers of neurons within a single model; and facts seem to be spread across many neurons. We revisit these objections by looking at what each neuron contributes to a model’s output, not just what causes it to fire, and we test our hypotheses by switching neurons off or by moving their outputs to other layers. We find that a neuron will contribute two unrelated concepts at once in about 1% or fewer of the cases we sampled, and that a neuron’s output keeps roughly the same meaning across most layers. We also find that although it usually takes changing many neurons to make a model get a fact wrong, the neurons involved generally represent concepts related to that fact, implying that facts, although distributed, are still readable.

Figure 1. One neuron adds John in two unrelated facts. L28 n2760 in Llama-3.1-8B-Instruct adds John for the password-cracking tool John the Ripper and for the author of the fourth Gospel. The automated description of when it activates (Choi et al., 2024), the kind used in much of past work, does not mention John. Only its negative activations occur with the gate open, so it adds − w .

# Introduction

Most interpretability tools today are built on learned features (sparse autoencoders and transcoders), on residual-stream directions (probes, steering vectors, lenses), or on separate models that describe activations in natural language. Few are built on neurons. The move away from neurons followed three observations. First, neurons activate on many unrelated inputs (Olah et al., 2020; Elhage et al., 2022; Gurnee et al., 2023; Bricken et al., 2023), automated explanations of them often fit poorly (Bills et al., 2023), and explanations change with the dataset (Bolukbasi et al., 2021). Second, representations appear to change from layer to layer (Belrose et al., 2023; Lindsey et al., 2024; Balcells et al., 2024; Lawson et al., 2025). Third, some computations, such as fact recall, appear to be spread over many neurons (Nanda et al., 2023; Chughtai et al., 2024). Taken at face value, these observations suggest that individual neurons would be uninterpretable because of superposition, relating neurons across layers would be hard because layers would not share coordinates, and removing or editing a fact could be very difficult.

However, by construction, the function a neuron implements is relatively straightforward. The activation of an MLP neuron is one context-dependent scalar, and the neuron adds that scalar times one fixed vector (its column of the down projection) to the residual stream. A neuron can thus be thought of as a context-gated steering vector. The scalar can be positive or negative, so a neuron adds its output vector with either sign, and the two signs can mean different things (Figure 1).

Motivated by this, we interpret each neuron’s output vector, the direction it adds to the residual stream (also called its output weights or value vector; Geva et al., 2022; Gurnee et al., 2024), and combine it with the contexts in which the neuron activates to form a hypothesis about the neuron’s function. To do so, we use the J-lens of Gurnee et al. (2026) to find the tokens each output vector makes the model most likely to produce. We test the hypotheses produced via the J-lens and activation contexts with interventions: ablating neuron activation values, injecting their output vectors at other layers, and steering with them. We first discuss how to interpret a neuron’s output vector through its vocabulary readout, and measure how often these readouts can be expected to be accurate and interpretable. We then examine the three observations in turn: neurons that activate on unrelated inputs, concepts that appear to drift across layers, and facts that appear to be spread over many neurons.

Contributions.

- We measure how much of each neuron’s output vector the J-lens can read, for every neuron in four models, and find that readouts match the text a neuron activates on far more often than chance.

- We propose a taxonomy of polysemanticity that covers both when a neuron activates and what it adds. Neurons that add two unrelated concepts are rare (about 1% or fewer), but we find the first known examples of them.

- We show that neurons write in an approximately fixed basis across layers, and that a concept changes with depth, likely because later neurons add new facets of it.

# Worse Together: How Performance Breaks Down in Multi-User Multi-Agent Teams

Sahan Paliskara 1
Nattaput Namchittai 1 , Jacqueline Tay 2 , and Avery Griffin 3
Andrew Lampinen 3
November 11, 2026

1 Anthropic Fellows Program; 2 Independent; 3 Anthropic

tl;dr
As AI agents become more capable and widely used, they are increasingly required to interact with each other. Users give their agents tasks which require them to share resources with other people’s agents; for instance, a compute budget, or a codebase, or the money for a group food order. These settings are understudied, so we built four environments with simulated users and everyday tasks and tested frontier models from Anthropic, OpenAI and Alibaba in them. In all four environments, group outcomes were worse when each user delegated to their own agent rather than when one agent served everyone. In these simulated settings, we also saw problematic behaviors that varied considerably by model and environment, including stalling as teams grow, overriding other users’ requests, and making unsupported claims about other people. Fixes depended on the environment: having a designated team leader and clearly stated priorities improved performance when agents shared a budget, while blocking agents from placing an order until they had read their messages rescued more failed group orders than simply rerunning them.

We are releasing three of the environments as a benchmark, MAMUBench, so that others can use them to test how well agents coordinate, and how they behave, in multi-user, multi-agent systems.

📄 Paper · 💻 Code

Research done as part of the Anthropic Fellows Program .

# Introduction

As AI agents become more common, users increasingly deploy them to pursue goals that require interacting with other agents. If you're reading this, you've probably had Claude run an experiment, book something, or write code in a shared codebase and merge the changes on GitHub. SemiAnalysis projected that Claude Code would author 20% or more of daily commits by the end of 2026. Features like Claude Tag and cross-session messaging point toward a world in which people delegate more tasks to agents—and those agents increasingly run into one another. Recent releases also let several users share resources through their agents: with the DoorDash CLI , several people's agents can add to one group cart; Slack Code brings agents such as Claude, Devin and GitHub Copilot into channels the whole team works in; and OpenAI's dots give each person an agent that works on their behalf, in a space shared with teammates (DevDay 2026 recap ). In each of these cases, every agent acts on behalf of its own user, and it is unclear how the agents should act for the group as a whole.

Recent work has found that multi-agent systems can suffer from coordination failures and other issues, largely in settings where agents pursue a shared objective. This raises the question of what happens when agents instead represent different users with different goals and preferences. We study these increasingly common settings, which we call multi-user, multi-agent systems. In our environments, each user has their own goal, and all of the users draw on one shared resource. We evaluate a range of frontier models from Anthropic, OpenAI, and Alibaba on these environments. We score the agents the way we would score a group of people negotiating over that resource: by the outcome for the group as a whole.

**Publication date:** The report is dated only "November 2026." It gives no specific day. The Mitel advisory it references was published on 16 November 2026.

**AI API services:**
- Sampled network traffic from the actor's server (204.76.203[.]204) reached two commercial AI API services between 7 and 17 November 2026, for a combined 155 hours.
- The services are not named. The traffic went to AWS-hosted endpoints.
- APEX Labs has moderate confidence the actor used the services. It cannot say exactly how, because the telemetry is sampled. Possible uses include data triage, exploitation or web-shell support, and preparing extortion material.
- The AI traffic restarted in the same second as the authentication-bypass request, after more than eight hours of silence.
- About 10% of sampled AI traffic occurred in hours with no sampled operator traffic.

**Timeline (confirmed victim, from first observed request):**
- T+1 min: authentication bypass
- T+9 min: two file uploads accepted
- T+12 min: first web-shell command
- T+15 to 30 min: escalation to root
- T+32 min: LDAPS bind to a domain controller using the LDAP connector's credentials
- T+53 min: first network logon with the directory account
- T+1.5 h: Kerberoasting script run
- T+2 h: authentication to multiple domain controllers in just over two minutes

- The 2026 advisory (MISA-2026-0012) covers five flaws: MTLVULN-1861, -1862, -1863, -1864, and -1877. MTLVULN-1864 is a blind command injection with a CVSS score of 10.0. No CVE IDs are given for these.

== 2026-11-26 v1 10.64898/2026.11.24.768376 Do single-cell foundation models need 512 dimensions for one number?
Single-cell foundation models represent counts through high-dimensional value embeddings or ranked feature tokens. We asked how many dimensions counts need and what network computes. In a controlled Transformer, a four-dimensional value track separated from a wide gene-identity backbone retains nearly all masked-prediction net gain; a straight line replaces pretrained value curves with little transfer loss. Across evaluated cohorts, clamping detected-gene values retains most gain in annotation, surface-protein prediction and perturbation-shift consistency, consistent with the prevalence of single-molecule counts. A two-feature encoder combining tie-free rank and within-cell standardized magnitude improves controlled retraining and preserves annotation when grafted onto pretrained scGPT. Gene offsets and three linear cell-level scalars approximate masked prediction and predict responses to count thinning; depth leads in the controlled model, while cell type leads in scGPT. Matched controls show that attribution, attention, dictionary and probe readouts can reflect depth, gene frequency, hub degree or directions that transfer little output.

== 2026-11-26 v1 10.64898/2026.11.23.768763 RIPPLE: learning nucleotide relations in an RNA foundation model
RNA function depends on interactions between nucleotides that can be widely separated in sequence, yet capturing these relationships remains challenging for RNA language models. Existing approaches primarily learn nucleotide relationships implicitly from individual nucleotide reconstruction or rely on external structural information to model nucleotide interactions. Here we introduce RIPPLE, an RNA foundation model that learns to identify and represent sparse, predictively useful nucleotide relationships directly from sequence. Pretrained on 32.4 million RNA sequences, RIPPLE uses pairwise predictive utility to guide relational learning, transferring training-time supervision into a sequence-only model without requiring structural inputs at inference. RIPPLE improves overall performance across five downstream tasks spanning RNA family classification, ribosome loading prediction, secondary-structure prediction, three-dimensional contact prediction, and splice-site recognition. Mechanistic analyses further show that utility-guided learning improves the recovery of informative interactions and enhances the transferability of learned RNA representations.

== 2026-11-26 v1 10.64898/2026.11.25.769078 Auditable AI agents for verifiable end-to-end scientific analysis
Artificial intelligence (AI) agents are evolving from research assistants into end-to-end executors, yet their capacity to generate conclusions at scale outpaces rigorous verification. Here we introduce an auditability-centred paradigm for scientific automation, wherein trust relies not on generative capability or self-evaluation, but on whether claims can be independently traced to primary evidence, reviewed and corrected. Moving beyond post-hoc checks, we embed verification throughout the research lifecycle via four principles: grounded knowledge, bounded execution, evidence-backed results and independent verification. We instantiate this paradigm in EvoTrace for viral evolutionary analysis. Distilling peer-review critiques and methodological literature, we curated 13 principles, 236 pitfalls and 50 analytical units - validating 47 across a six-tier hierarchy - to encode methodological limits as executable constraints. Across simulated benchmarks, six viral datasets and an end-to-end Crimean-Congo haemorrhagic fever virus (CCHFV) study, claim-evidence auditing compiled evidence packages for all 233 analyses (flagging 26 incomplete evidentiary chains), while independent numerical and figure audits rectified 17 flaws, including three blocker-level errors. For CCHFV, EvoTrace intercepted a data-contradictory claim, recalibrating 'no reassortment candidates' to 'no high-confidence candidates'. By co-delivering verification evidence, auditable automation shifts AI-driven science

Abstract: Agent skills are directories of instructions, reference materials, and scripts loaded on demand by coding agents. According to SkillsBench, although human-curated skills can raise the passing rate by about 16.6 percentage points (pp) on average, they have actually reduced the results for some tasks. Abstract: Influence functions are a promising way to identify which training examples are responsible for a model's output. # Title: Sparse-to-Sparse Feature Learning for Cross-Layer Analysis and Steering
Authors: Masahiro Kaneko , Ayana Niwa , Timothy Baldwin
View a PDF of the paper titled Sparse-to-Sparse Feature Learning for Cross-Layer Analysis and Steering, by Masahiro Kaneko and 2 other authors
View PDF
