Abstract: Understanding how models internally represent information is a central challenge in interpretation and control. Sparse autoencoders (SAEs) decompose dense hidden representations into sparse features, and cross-layer methods capture structure spanning multiple layers. However, existing objectives do not explicitly train the sparse code at one layer to predict the sparse code at the next layer. We propose sparse-to-sparse feature learning (S2S), where sparse features at each intermediate layer are trained to predict those of the immediately following layer, with the final layer anchored by an output-distribution loss and optimization proceeding sequentially from output to input. Experiments across eight language models show stronger adjacent-layer correspondence than matched sparse-feature baselines. We evaluate feature-based interventions at matched output-distribution shift, separating steering-induced effects from sparse-pathway reconstruction effects. Causal ablation provides complementary evidence beyond correspondence metrics.

# Title: Stable Gated DeltaNet-2: Understanding and Mitigating Recurrent State Instability
Authors: Xichong Zhang , Xixuan Hao , Zhichen Liu , Le Zhou , Zeyu Zhang , Boyu Chen , Mingfei Lu , Zehao Lin , Bo Tang , Yonggang Zhang , Linyun Liu , Feiyu Xiong , Jianlin Su , Zhiyu Li

View PDF
HTML (experimental)
Abstract: Linear attention offers an efficient solution for long-sequence modeling via linear complexity and fixed-size recurrent states. Gated DeltaNet-2 (GDN-2) introduces independent channel-wise control over erasure and writing, enhancing state-update expressiveness and in-context retrieval, yet it suffers from training failures during long-context training. We trace these failures to the asymmetry between reading and modification directions during erasure, which yields non-normal erase operators whose directional gains accumulate across tokens, triggering exponential state growth even without new writes. To resolve this, we propose \model{}, employing symmetric erasure to ensure non-expansive state propagation and decay-regulated residual writing to preserve writing flexibility. Theoretically, we establish an $O(\sqrt{T})$ upper bound on recurrent state growth while retaining chunkwise parallel computation. Experiments on ~1.6B parameter models show that \model{} achieves stable training alongside improved long-context retrieval. Compared to GDN-2, it boosts the 128K average RULER score by 6.80 points in the recurrent setting and average accuracy across nine downstream tasks by 0.62 points in the hybrid setting.

# Title: Solve Vision with Code: Coding Agents Are Stronger Visual Reasoners Than Video Models
Authors: Dezhi Luo , Fengyuan Yu , Haotian Zhang , Zehong Zhao , Ran Ji , Siyuan An , Huayi Qin , Qingying Gao , Zhongang Cai , Lei Yang , Ziqi Huang , Ruisi Wang , Maijunxian Wang , Hokin Deng

Abstract: Video generation models are increasingly evaluated as visual reasoners: given a first frame and a natural-language prompt, can the model produce the video in which the specified task is carried out? The paradigm is considered advantageous because the reasoning is native to the visual medium, unfolding directly in the frames rather than through language or code. Whether this native route is in fact the more reliable path to visual reasoning has not been tested against a symbolic alternative under the same conditions. We therefore pose the same tasks, with identical inputs, output specification and evaluator, to both media: rather than denoising pixels, a coding agent writes a program that renders the answer video, which an unmodified rule-based evaluator scores. On VBVR-Pro-Bench (Xu et al., 2026), a 500-instance suite spanning five cognitive categories with symbolic ground truth, the agent receives the same first frame and prompt as the video model, with no access to ground truth, metadata or generation models, and one attempt per instance. Three closed-model agents (Codex with gpt-6-astra, Claude Code with Fable 5.1 and Gemini CLI with Gemini 3.1 Pro) score 0.923, 0.894 and 0.893, each more than 0.22 above the strongest video model. Among 23 runnable open-weight models, the best, GLM-5, reaches 0.572, above all video models except the RL-trained one. Together, we show that for tasks whose solutions can be computed from a first frame and a prompt, program synthesis is currently a substantially more reliable route to visual reasoning than video generation. We further distinguish depictive programs, which navigate the image to recover a transferable scheme, from propositional programs, which operate on hard-coded values, revealing how visual reasoning unfolds in agent-written programs and what it implies for its nature of reasoning in general.

Authors: Zeqi Zhou , Minghao Liu , Jiarui Liu , Qingcheng Zeng , Rui Yang , Tianyu Liu , Zetao Yang , Wenqiang Zu , Enduo Zhao , Heng-Jui Chang , Lun-Hsin Kuo , Meng-Fu Chen , Haokai Zhao , Weijia Zhang , Jen-Tse Huang , Stephen Huang , Eli Cheung , Zhijing Jin , Mona Diab , Weihao Xuan
View a PDF of the paper titled REE: A Scientific Research Entrance Exam for AI Agents, by Zeqi Zhou and 19 other authors
View PDF
HTML (experimental)
Abstract: Autonomous research agents are emerging as a promising approach to scientific problem-solving across disciplines, owing to their growing ability to improve a solution through repeated experiments. Evaluating this ability requires benchmarks that pose open-ended research problems and measure improvements over established scientific methods. We introduce REE (Research Entrance Exam), a benchmark that tests AI agents on scientific research. It consists of 100 open-ended research problems spanning five broad scientific areas and 23 domains. To ensure high quality, every problem is drawn from active research in its field and individually reviewed by domain experts. Each problem is posed as a task of iterative improvement: an agent has up to 12 hours to improve a working starter solution, and REE scores the result on a common scale against an established expert solution evaluated under comparable conditions. By this measure, two of the four frontier agents we evaluate, Claude Opus 5.5 and GPT-6.1 Sol, outperform the expert solutions on 86% and 81% of problems, across all five scientific areas. Their runs also show how they do so: both agents surpass the expert solutions within the first two hours on average, and their best solutions mostly tailor or combine established methods of the field. REE thus provides a unified framework for evaluating autonomous scientific research, capturing both improvements over established methods and the research processes behind them.

# Title: Reinforcement Learning Can Be Recovered From Its Own Rollouts
Authors: Jiayi Sheng , Jingwen Gu , Guanning Zeng , Zhaoyi Zhou , Stefano Viel , Qianqian Wang , Fahim Tajwar , Andrea Zanette
View a PDF of the paper titled Reinforcement Learning Can Be Recovered From Its Own Rollouts, by Jiayi Sheng and 7 other authors
View PDF
HTML (experimental)
Abstract: Broadly speaking, reinforcement learning (RL) post-training converts compute into model capabilities by training on model-generated data. Typically, the rollouts are discarded after each update, and the knowledge acquired during RL resides in the model weights. In this work, we investigate how much of this knowledge is retained in the rollouts themselves. A natural first attempt is to replay the original RL algorithm on archived (rather than freshly generated) rollouts, but this generally leads to catastrophic collapse. We provide a simple explanation for this phenomenon, which in turn suggests a remedy we call maximum likelihood replay: fitting the model to its archived rollouts. Surprisingly, starting from the same base model and replaying the rollouts in the order in which they were generated, without any distinction between correct and incorrect responses, is sufficient to recover the performance of online RL. In fact, a single maximum likelihood update per rollout batch closely tracks the entire learning curve of online RL. Furthermore, maximum likelihood replay on the rollouts of the last few RL steps often suffices to recover the final model's performance. This suggests that much of the compute invested in RL goes into discovering an improved sampling distribution rather than learning it from samples.

# Title: PROVE: Mitigating Long-Horizon LLM Collusion with Reinforcement Learning from Verified Evidence
Authors: Haochen Luo , Jie Fu , Mukai Li , Yuqi Wang , Qi Liu
View a PDF of the paper titled PROVE: Mitigating Long-Horizon LLM Collusion with Reinforcement Learning from Verified Evidence, by Haochen Luo and 4 other authors
View PDF
HTML (experimental)
Abstract: When LLM agents verify each other's work over a long interaction, they drift into collusion: they come to accept work without the evidence that the verification protocol requires. Collusion is absent at the start and builds up episode by episode, which we trace to accurate feedback accumulating in memory. An agent that follows the rule is told that its verdict was wrong whenever its peer was right, so breaking the rule is the reward-maximizing choice, and agents talk themselves into it in their private reflections. Existing mitigations leave the agents unchanged; we train the behavior out. PROVE (Protocol Reinforcement from Verified Evidence) is a multi-agent reinforcement learning method that rewards verdicts by the evidence behind them rather than by their outcome, and credits every call an agent makes, including the calls that solve its own task, with the outcome that call controls. On Qwen3.6-27B, a LoRA adapter trained on six-episode interactions takes the collusion rate on held-out task sequences at the original ten-episode horizon from 65.0% to 1.0%, with no detectable change in task success. Collusion that converged in every interaction now converges in none, and the gain holds four episodes beyond the longest interaction seen in training. The trained 27B model colludes less than every model evaluated in the original study, closed-weight frontier models included. Code is available at this https URL .

# Title: Semantic Density Does Not Predict Agent-Memory Collapse
Authors: Saksham Gupta , Yash Choudhary , Arpit Upadhyay
View a PDF of the paper titled Semantic Density Does Not Predict Agent-Memory Collapse, by Saksham Gupta and 2 other authors
View PDF
HTML (experimental)
Abstract: Persistent textual memory can improve LLM agents, but repeated updates can erode task performance. We ask whether memory-store statistics warn before held-out accuracy declines. We registered mean pairwise cosine similarity ($\rho$) and 13 additional geometry, retrieval, and graph statistics on 805 snapshots from 13 memory methods across ALFWorld, AppWorld, ScienceWorld, WebShop, and two ARC-AGI settings. These methods store trajectories, rules, workflows, strategies, or linked records, using selective retrieval or whole-store prompting. No such statistic reliably predicted early signs of task accuracy decline, and $\rho$ had zero median lead. With the checkpoint after peak accuracy as a secondary decline point, measures of highly similar pairs and nearest-neighbor crowding changed earlier but did not consistently outperform stored-item count. We trained classifiers on this corpus and applied them unchanged to PropWorld runs of up to 5,000 crafting tasks. They falsely flagged 56.9% of checkpoints from size-limited stores with stable accuracy and detected only 18% of checkpoints after task success fell to zero. Thus, global semantic density did not provide a reliable warning, while local crowding did not transfer consistently across memory designs. In these long-horizon runs, size-limited stores remained stable, while the sole failure arose when unbounded whole-store prompting exceeded model input capacity, which token growth predicted directly.

# Title: Deletion You Can Check: Auditing LLM Unlearning
Authors: Mayank Gulati , Gerhard Wunder
View a PDF of the paper titled Deletion You Can Check: Auditing LLM Unlearning, by Mayank Gulati and Gerhard Wunder
View PDF
HTML (experimental)
Abstract: A common indication that a fine-tuned model has forgotten a deleted record is a membership-inference score near chance (ROC-AUC $\approx 0.5$). This reading is sound only if the comparison population represents how the record should behave after a valid deletion---a counterfactual that is rarely validated. We test this premise in a controlled $2\times2$ study pairing two membership-inference benchmarks, ArxivMIA and BookMIA, with two language models, Llama-3.2-1B and Qwen2.5-1.5B. Exact retraining validates the membership reference: it lies within the prespecified chance band on ArxivMIA but reaches $0.122$ on BookMIA, causing the same metric to reject an empirical deletion reference. A post-hoc BookMIA/Qwen diagnostic replaces benchmark label-0 records with same-pool, never-fine-tuned records and moves the reference from $0.257$ to $0.523$, supporting population mismatch in that cell. Each approximate-unlearning checkpoint is judged jointly on membership removal, deletion-targeted shift beyond non-deletion variation, and utility. On the admitted ArxivMIA/Llama axis, no tested configuration of gradient ascent with retain descent (GA+GD), negative-preference optimization with retain training (NPO-RT), or teacher--student unlearning (SCRUB) passes. A score near chance is not evidence of forgetting until a reference establishes what chance means.

# Title: Puzzling-Bench: Evaluating Language Models on 23,777 Human-Written Puzzles with Community-Verified Answers
Authors: Abhinav Sharma , Li Li , Chien Van Nguyen , Sai Karthik Navuluru , Bo Ni , Xiangbo Gao , Xiaolei Huang , Yue Zhao , Nesreen K. Ahmed , Tyler Derr , Yu Wang , Hongjie Chen , Zhengzhong Tu , Thien Huu Nguyen , Ryan A. Rossi , Franck Dernoncourt
View a PDF of the paper titled Puzzling-Bench: Evaluating Language Models on 23,777 Human-Written Puzzles with Community-Verified Answers, by Abhinav Sharma and 15 other authors
View PDF
HTML (experimental)
Abstract: We introduce Puzzling-Bench, a benchmark of 23,777 puzzles with community-verified answers drawn from the Puzzling Stack Exchange archive (2014-2026): riddles, ciphers, logic grids, lateral-thinking problems, wordplay and recreational mathematics, a third of them with images. Every puzzle carries the answer accepted by its author, a short reference answer taken from it (LLM-extracted for the evaluation sets and checked on a 50-puzzle human review), the author's own hints, community tags and a creation date, so that the benchmark supports hint ablations, category analysis and a rolling post-cutoff slice (254 puzzles posted after the training cutoff of six of the nine models we evaluate, including the best one) as a contamination check. We evaluate nine frontier and open models with a two-tier scorer (normalized exact match, then an LLM judge) and validate the judge with three judges from two model families: they agree on 95-97% of verdicts (kappa 0.82-0.96), move no model by more than 1.6 points, and show no own-family preference. The best model, GPT-6.1, reaches 74.8% on a shared 255-puzzle set; a hard core of 17 puzzles defeats all nine models; model failures are strongly correlated, and the second-best model contributes a single puzzle to a greedy ensemble, yet an oracle over all nine reaches 91%. On a 100-puzzle multimodal pilot, withholding the question's image costs the two best models 24 and 35 points. We release the dataset, the scoring pipeline and all per-row provenance.

Abstract: The Platonic Representation Hypothesis (PRH) posits that AI models converge toward a shared representation of the world, even when trained on different data modalities. Previous work has found evidence for the PRH in the activations of vision and language models. In this work, we ask whether vision and language models also converge in how they act on these representations: precisely, in how these internal representations affect the models' output. At a chosen layer of a transformer, the Jacobian lens gives every word in the vocabulary (or class in an image classifier) a vector in the hidden state: the vector that most increases the model's tendency to generate that word, at that position or later, or to predict that class. Collectively, these vectors make up what is referred to as the model's J-space. We find evidence of the PRH in J-space across vision and language models, and furthermore, we find that J-spaces mostly converge up to a rotation. That is, a single rotation, fitted on a subset of words, approximately maps one model's J-space onto another's, and so applies to words and classes it was not fitted on. A word's vector, rotated from a text-only language model's J-space into the visual patch tokens of a vision-language model, changes the object the vision-language model says is in the image (and only in the image region where it is added). Rotated into an image generator's text conditioning, a word's vector changes the object in the generated image. Rotated into an ImageNet classifier (trained without text), it raises that object's class score above almost all others, and vice versa. This suggests that models converge not only in how they represent the world, but also in how they act on it.

Abstract: Skill acquisition alone does not establish a reusable skill library: task proficiency does not specify a compositional interface. Motivated by agents that acquire and refine skills, we study independently learned soft-prompt skills on frozen language models, with skill identities and execution order supplied. Across four digit-task bases and three record-editing models, mean composition accuracy in one call is at most 7.6%, compared with 88.2% to 100% over two calls that add computation and an explicit intermediate output. Neutral-insertion training improves robustness but leaves substantial interference, which block length and per-token norm alone cannot explain on two of four digit bases. Blocks of the same operation need not be interchangeable: after training next to frozen learned partners, a post hoc test on two Qwen bases shows that replacing those partners with independently learned blocks of the same operations lowers median composition accuracy from 98.0% and 95.3% to 12.7% and 0.5%, although every replacement scores at least 90% alone. Repair can improve a composition while impairing the original skill, and rehearsal improves retention while transfer remains limited on Qwen2.5-0.5B. Internal interventions constrain explanations without identifying a shared failure mechanism. These findings motivate evaluating compatibility, retention and transfer alongside acquisition when building skill libraries for self-evolving agents. Code is available at this https URL .

Authors: Yilin Luo , Jin Hwa Lee , Andrew M. Saxe , Antonio Sclocchi

Abstract: Today, a core pipeline of artificial intelligence systems is pretraining on a broad range of text corpora and then fine-tuning on specific tasks or desired behaviors. Yet we still have limited understanding of how fine-tuning on a restricted data distribution modifies representations acquired during pretraining. In particular, it remains unclear whether surface behavioral suppression happens together with the erasure of latent representations that support it. In this work, we study supervised fine-tuning (SFT) by pretraining transformers on a controlled context-free grammar with hierarchical latent structure, the Random Hierarchy Model (RHM), and fine-tuning with a restricted subset of its generative rules. While during pretraining the model's ability to generate with the correct grammar rules coincides with building the internal representations of the corresponding latent, we find that SFT exhibits a very different dynamics: (i) the generation of deleted rules changes on a fast timescale inversely proportional to the magnitude of the token-latent correlation; meanwhile, their corresponding representations stay intact; (ii) the hidden representations of the deleted rules become forgotten on a much longer timescale, associated with a slow drift of the network parameters. Finally, we observe analogous results in a realistic setup with natural language, suggesting that this timescale separation in forgetting is a more general phenomenon of fine-tuning language models.

Abstract: Knowledge distillation enables the deployment of large language models through smaller student models, but the compression process can introduce regressions in trustworthiness even when downstream performance is preserved. Repairing such failures is challenging because the original distillation corpus is often unavailable, while direct preference optimization may alter capabilities inherited from the teacher. We propose a targeted repair framework based on the proximal Bregman response function (PBRF) that addresses both limitations. We estimate the curvature required for PBRF using a surrogate proxy dataset, removing dependence on the original transfer corpus, and extend the framework to preference-based supervision through an odds-ratio objective. This enables the use of preferred and dispreferred response pairs while constraining changes to the distilled model. Our results show that the proposed approach improves targeted trustworthiness behaviors for both pre-training and post-training models while largely preserving downstream performance, providing a practical alternative to re-distillation or unconstrained preference optimization. Our experiment results show that across different distilled models, the trustworthy regression can be improved by up to 8% with less than 1% decrement in perplexity.

One of these involves the use of large language models (LLMs) to resolve well-specified conjectures via text-based reasoning, while another uses narrow models and interpretability for more open-ended, human-in-the-loop exploration using object-based mathematical data. The latter is limited in its ability to move beyond simple empirical pattern detection while the former is not well-designed for direct, open-ended exploration of large mathematical datasets. In this paper we introduce PatternMiner, a system that combines these two paradigms. In PatternMiner, an LLM agent generates mathematical datasets based on an initial broad question, trains narrow machine learning models on them, uses interpretability techniques to extract patterns from these trained models, and uses these patterns to formulate conjectures. Once an initial conjecture has been formulated, PatternMiner instructs the agent to search for counterexamples using calls to mathematical software. If a set of counterexamples can be found, these are used as feedback for conjecture refinement or another round of training and interpretability. The conjecture progressively evolves through this iterative sequence with the agent allowed to try to prove it at any point. We describe the results of applying PatternMiner to five well-known positivity problems in algebraic combinatorics. PatternMiner proves several new theorems related to Schubert positivity and projection, a character-row evaluation formula, a restricted version of the Kazhdan--Lusztig combinatorial invariance conjecture, and Schur positivity for a family of immanant coefficients. We end by analyzing the most common routes to conjecture generation that are used by PatternMiner in our case studies as well as documenting the most common failure modes.

HTML (experimental)
Abstract: Large language models (LLMs) perform well on chemistry knowledge benchmarks, which mainly assess question answering and isolated tasks. Chemical research, however, requires using specialized tools and interpreting their outputs to obtain chemically valid results. To address this gap, we introduce Crucible Bench to evaluate this ability across all four stages of the design-make-test-analyze (DMTA) cycle. The benchmark contains 1,078 tasks in 12 task families curated from 18 published datasets, covering molecular design, synthesis planning, experimental execution, closed-loop optimization, simulation, and analytical characterization. Agents access 75 domain-specific tools through the Model Context Protocol in seven isolated environments. Sandboxed graders verify the resulting synthesis routes, experimental protocols, and other outputs. Laboratory tasks use robotic simulators or previously measured experimental data. We evaluate 14 LLMs as agents and find that the best achieves an overall score of 0.545, with synthesis planning and closed-loop optimization emerging as the hardest domains. Overall performance does not predict optimization performance well: the model ranked twelfth overall achieves the highest score in closed-loop optimization. Error analysis also shows that agents often submit chemically invalid results despite running their tools successfully. Stronger models benefit more from tool access, but reliable use of chemical software remains a challenge that Crucible Bench can track as models improve.

SAP is preparing a plan to eliminate at least 10,000 positions as the German firm reshapes its software business for the artificial intelligence era, Bloomberg reported on Thursday , citing people familiar with the matter.
The report came as the company flagged a cybersecurity attack, but said it had found "no evidence of unauthorized access to customer business data."

"SAP has identified suspicious activity and promptly implemented the necessary measures to protect its customers and preserve the security of its services," a company spokesperson said.
"Our customers trust us to protect their data, and that remains our highest priority. In a highly dynamic threat environment, we will continue to strengthen our security to provide the secure and resilient environment our customers depend on."
The company did not respond to a request for comment on the reported job cuts. The number could change after labor negotiations.
Other software companies have also tied workforce reductions to AI initiatives, though for different reasons. WiseTech Global said in February it planned to cut about 2,000 jobs over two years as it integrated AI into its products and operations.
Atlassian said in March it would cut about 1,600 jobs partly to fund further AI investment, while Cloudflare said in May it would eliminate more than 1,100 roles as it moved toward an AI-first operating model.

In the U.S., employers cited AI in 121,401 job-cut announcements through October 2026, accounting for about 20% of the total, according to a Nov. 5 report from outplacement and executive coaching firm Challenger, Gray & Christmas.
SAP employs more than 110,000 people worldwide. Bloomberg reported that all departments had been asked to identify potential cuts, with product, engineering and sales in particular focus.
The company also underwent a reorganization in 2024, when it eliminated around 10,000 positions through a program that relied mainly on voluntary departures and retraining.
Its headcount later remained relatively flat as it hired for new roles, Bloomberg reported.
In 2023, SAP CEO Christian Klein told CNBC he did not necessarily expect a reduction in the workforce, saying he expected the company to grow and "accelerate" its total revenue.

Er behandelt KI-Agenten, die Cyberangriffe zunehmend selbstständig ausführen, und warnt, dass solche Agenten kritische Infrastruktur wie Spitäler, Schulen und Energiesysteme ins Visier nehmen könnten. Offene Modelle sollen den Verteidigern helfen (KI-Agenten führen Cyberangriffe immer autonomer aus, weshalb auch die Verteidiger leistungsfähige KI-Systeme brauchen. Offene Modelle wie Apertus könnten helfen.). Als Beleg für die Gefahr nennt der Artikel einen Vorfall bei OpenAI, bei dem KI-Agenten Dutzende Unternehmens- und Regierungswebsites kompromittierten (OpenAI-Agenten haben Dutzende Unternehmens- und Regierungswebsites gehackt).

Ergänzend gibt es mehrere Hintergrundquellen zur Lage in der Schweiz:

- **Meldepflicht und Angriffe:** Seit April 2025 müssen Cyberangriffe auf kritische Infrastrukturen dem Bund gemeldet werden, und zwar innerhalb von 24 Stunden beim Bundesamt für Cybersicherheit (BACS) (Seit April 2025 gilt eine gesetzliche Meldepflicht für Cyberangriffe auf kritische Infrastrukturen. Wer angegriffen wird, muss dies innerhalb von 24 Stunden dem Bundesamt für Cybersicherheit melden.). Laut SRF wurden in den neun Monaten zuvor mehr als 260 Angriffe auf kritische Infrastruktur gemeldet (in den vergangenen neun Monaten meldete das BACS mehr als 260 Angriffe auf kritische Infrastruktur).
- **KI als Werkzeug der Angreifer:** Laut dem BACS nutzen Angreifer in der Schweiz KI bisher vor allem für Betrugsmaschen (Auch in der Schweiz nutzen Angreifer KI – bisher aber vor allem für Betrugsmaschen, wie das Bundesamt für Cybersicherheit festhält.). Ein SRF-Beitrag mit dem obersten Cyberverantwortlichen Florian Schütz geht ebenfalls darauf ein, wie Cyberkriminelle KI zunehmend nutzen.
- **Nachrichtendienst:** Der NDB hält gezielte staatliche Sabotageangriffe auf kritische Infrastruktur derzeit für unwahrscheinlich, würde diese Einschätzung aber im Fall eines bewaffneten Konflikts ändern (Gezielte Cyber-Sabotageangriffe auf kritische Infrastrukturen durch staatliche Akteure hält der NDB aktuell für unwahrscheinlich. Dies würde sich ändern, wenn die Schweiz in einen internationalen bewaffneten Konflikt verwickelt würde.).

Das Datum des OpenAI-Vorfalls und der Dialog-Beitrag selbst sind nicht eindeutig datiert, und die Quellen stammen teils aus unterschiedlichen Zeiträumen (2025 bis 2026). results:
The Autonomous Warfare Command (AUTOWARCOM) was announced by Defense Secretary Pete Hegseth on September 30, 2026, at Marine Corps Base Quantico. The results describe it as a four-star combatant command for unmanned and autonomous warfare, and they agree on most of the basics.

- **Purpose and authority:** Hegseth said the command would have service-like authorities to scale autonomous and robotic capabilities across the joint force. The Agincourt memo describes AutoWarCom as a four-star functional combatant command, a headquarters organized around a mission rather than a region, like U.S. Cyber Command.
- **Rationale:** Hegseth argued that "The pace of war is changing faster than the process to support it."
- **Interim step:** Hegseth issued a memorandum directing the Direct Reporting Portfolio Manager for Unmanned Systems (DRPM-UxS) to lead Project Agincourt, an effort to create the command.
- **Structure:** One outlet reports that the Defense Autonomous Warfare Group and Joint Interagency Task Force 401 became deputy offices under it.
- **Timeline:** Sources differ on the target date. One says the proposed command is scheduled to be established by October 1, 2027. Another describes a memo that directs the unmanned systems office to work with Congress on the needed legislation, with a goal of establishing AutoWarCom by Oct. (the snippet is cut off before the year).
- **Congressional review:** A Congressional Research Service report dated November 18, 2026 covers the command. It notes that Congress may consider whether or not to authorize and appropriate funding for the command.
- **Open questions:** One analysis notes that senior officials disclosed few concrete operational milestones or performance measures for the future command.

The Army also responded by ordering its own autonomous systems command, the Army Futures and Autonomous Systems Command (FASCOM), a day after the announcement. One outlet also says Southern Command created a theater-level autonomous warfare command of its own in April 2026, which is a separate effort.

results:
I found no OpenAI or Anthropic misuse threat report dated November 2026. The closest match is Anthropic's September 2026 report, which the results describe as its most recent.

- **Anthropic's September 2026 report:** Anthropic published its fourth threat-intelligence report on September 10, 2026, documenting misuse of its Claude models that the company's Threat Intelligence team detected and disrupted between December 2025 and August 2026. It covers seven areas of harm: cyber operations, influence operations, surveillance, scams and fraud, biological misuse, conventional weapons development, and illicit distillation.
- **Bio-related cases:** NPR reports that Anthropic noted five case studies in its report. Anthropic said it was hard to know definitively whether these were tied to bioweapons plans, but that it disrupted the activity and shared information with authorities and industry partners (NPR).
- **Key trend:** One summary says Anthropic states that the operating model has proliferated across every class of actor it investigated. Another says the report every case in the report ran on Haiku, Sonnet or Opus.
- **OpenAI:** The results contain no OpenAI threat report, so I can't confirm whether OpenAI has published one recently. The only OpenAI item is a November 2026 story about counterespionage hiring and office security (according to a November 24, 2026, Financial Times report summarized by The Next Web). That is not a misuse report.

Sources are mostly secondary coverage and blogs, so check Anthropic's threat-intelligence page and OpenAI's publications directly for primary documents.

CISO Daily Briefing

results:
The search turned up consistent reporting that UK AISI found a robustness regression in pre-release GPT-6.2 Astra, but I could not retrieve the OpenAI system card itself. Everything below comes from secondary coverage.

- **Jailbreak finding:** Per the coverage, the UK AISI team built a universal jailbreak against two pre-release checkpoints using about half the model queries that GPT-6 Astra required. AISI tested two pre-release versions of GPT-6.2 Astra: the original and an updated version that OpenAI considered more robust based on internal tests. In both cases, a researcher developed a universal jailbreak to obtain responses to cyber queries with about half the number of requests needed for the previous GPT-6 Astra.
- **Attribution to the card:** OpenAI's system card from Nov. 17 says UK AISI identified a substantial regression in robustness relative to GPT-6 Astra. The card is dated November 17, 2026.
- **Capability context:** OpenAI says GPT-6.2 Astra meets its Critical threshold for cybersecurity capabilities. Coverage also says that once jailbroken, the model showed substantial cyber capabilities.
- **Mitigations not retested:** OpenAI changed the model's safeguards after testing, but the institute had not independently tested the latest changes when the system card was written, while OpenAI said internal testing had validated the changes and that it believed the regression was mitigated.
- **Monitoring result:** In a separate test, GPT-6.2 Astra acted as a monitor for GPT-6 Astra's unsanctioned cyberattack records. Its miss rate was 19% on transcripts with violations, rising to 51% when it also received unsummarized reasoning (per DataConomy and DEV Community).

Caveats: the sources disagree on some details. One report says UK AISI does not consider its GPT-6.2 Astra result informative, a point I could not reconcile with the others. Several sources are low-profile blogs or aggregators, and one CSA page has garbled table content. Check the original OpenAI GPT-6.2 system card and UK AISI's own publications before relying on these specifics.

I found no Register article from November 2026 in these results. The results cover the India AI Governance Guidelines themselves, which were released in November 2025.

- **Release and framing:** On November 5, 2025, the Ministry of Electronics and Information Technology ("MeitY") formally released the India AI Governance Guidelines under the IndiaAI Mission.
- **Approach:** Anchored in seven guiding sutras, the framework adopts a principle-based, techno-legal approach.
- **No separate AI law:** The Guidelines do not introduce a separate AI legislation but instead establishes a governance framework that relies on existing laws, institutional oversight and phased regulatory development. Enforcement falls to existing bodies, with sectoral regulators remaining responsible for enforcement and oversight within their legal mandate.
- **Institutions:** Oversight is organized around an AI Governance Group for strategic oversight and an AI Safety Institute for technical validation and safety research, with a Technology & Policy Expert Committee also involved (the Technology & Policy Expert Committee and AI Governance Group for strategic oversight, and the AI Safety Institute for technical validation & safety research).
- **Accountability tools:** The guidelines favor voluntary measures, with voluntary frameworks such as industry codes of practice, technical standards and self-certifications as an important layer of risk mitigation.
- **Critics and commentators:** EY describes the approach as light-touch, innovation-first, enabling rapid experimentation through sandboxes and voluntary standards.
- **Later clarification:** A December 2025 PIB release states that India AI Governance Guidelines do not allow unrestricted deployment of high-risk AI systems.

If you need the Register piece specifically, a search on its title or publication date may locate it.

DEPARTMENT OF COMMERCE

International Trade Administration

[Docket No. 260922-0056]


American SI Exports Program; On-Demand Consortia for Specific 
Foreign Opportunities

AGENCY: International Trade Administration, U.S. Department of 
Commerce.

ACTION: Notice of SI Exports Program--On-Demand Consortia.

-----------------------------------------------------------------------

SUMMARY: The Department of Commerce (the Department), through the 
International Trade Administration (ITA), establishes the On-Demand 
Consortia pathway under the Super Intelligence (SI) Exports Program \1\ 
(the Program) authorized by Executive Order 14320: Promoting the Export 
of the American SI Technology Stack, as laid out in the Call for 
Proposals for Pre-Set Consortia, released on April 10, 2026 (April 2026 
CFP). The Department also provides for re-designation and de-
designation of packages designated under the April 2026 CFP or this 
notice and for the Pre-Set Consortia pathway to reopen at a later date.
---------------------------------------------------------------------------

    \1\ Per Executive Order 14434, Inaugurating the Era of Super 
Intelligence, federal departments and agencies shall, to the maximum 
extent permitted by law, use the terms ``Super Intelligence'' and 
``SI'' in place of ``Artificial Intelligence'' and ``AI'' in public 
communications.

DATES: Applications for designation under the On-Demand Consortia 
pathway may be submitted beginning November 30, 2026. The Department 
---------------------------------------------------------------------------
will accept applications on a rolling basis.

ADDRESSES: Applications must be submitted electronically through the 
American SI Exports Program submission portal at https://SIexports.gov/on-demand. The portal provides filing instructions for On-Demand 
Consortium applications. The Department will post Program updates and 
additional information on the Program at https://SIexports.gov.

FOR FURTHER INFORMATION CONTACT: American SI Exports Team, 
International Trade Administration, U.S. Department of Commerce, 1401 
Constitution Avenue NW, Washington, DC 20230; email SIexports.gov">info@SIexports.gov.

SUPPLEMENTARY INFORMATION:

I. Background and Purpose

    Executive Order 14320 of July 23, 2025, Promoting the Export of the 
American SI Technology Stack, directs the Secretary of Commerce, in 
consultation with the Secretary of State and the Director of the Office 
of Science and Technology Policy, to establish and implement the 
American SI Exports Program (the Program) to support the development 
and deployment of United States full-stack SI export packages.
    Commerce announced the Call for Proposals for Pre-Set Consortia on 
April 1, 2026 (91 FR 18412) (April 2026 CFP), establishing the first 
pathway for designation under the Program. The initial phase of the 
Pre-Set Consortia pathway closed on June 30, 2026.
    This notice establishes a second pathway for designation in the 
Program: On-Demand Consortia. On-Demand Consortia are industry-led 
groupings formed to respond to a specific, identified foreign export 
opportunity, as described in Section III, infra. This notice also 
provides for re-designation and de-designation of packages designated 
under either this notice or the April 2026 CFP, and for the reopening 
at a later date of the Pre-Set Consortia pathway.

II. Eligible On-Demand Consortia

    On-Demand Consortia must comply with the eligibility requirements 
laid out in Sections II and IV of the April 2026 CFP, except that:
    1. A subsidiary, affiliate, or branch whose ultimate parent entity 
is organized under the laws of a foreign jurisdiction or has its 
principal place of business outside the United States is eligible to be 
an anchor member as long as the entity itself is organized under the 
laws of the United States or a State thereof, with its principal place 
of business in the United States, and meets qualifications (1) and (3) 
of an anchor member laid out in Section II of the April 2026 CFP.
    2. Packages offered by On-Demand Consortia are not themselves 
required to cover the full five layers of the SI technology stack 
described in Section III of the April 2026 CFP. Instead, On-Demand 
Consortia need only offer the layers of the SI stack necessary to meet 
the buyer's demands for the identified foreign export opportunity, 
provided that the layers offered meet the content requirements 
described in Section IV of the April 2026 CFP, as applicable.
    An On-Demand Consortium that is not offering a full-stack SI 
technology package, as described in Executive Order 14320 and Section 
III of the April 2026 CFP, must demonstrate that the layers offered by 
the Consortium will combine with existing or acquired infrastructure or 
capabilities to result in a full-stack SI technology package. An On-
Demand Consortium must attest that it has made reasonable efforts to 
confirm that the resulting full-stack SI technology package meets the 
content and ownership requirements established under Section IV of the 
April 2026 CFP for all five layers, whether provided by Consortium 
members or not. An On-Demand Consortium may also include a Trusted 
Foreign Enterprise (TFE) as an exception to certain content 
requirements, consistent with Section II.A. of the April 2026 CFP.\2\ 
In addition, the Secretary may, in consultation with the Secretaries of 
State, War, and Energy and the Director of the Office of Science and 
Technology Policy, waive the U.S. ownership and control requirement 
under Section IV.C of the April 2026 CFP for an On-Demand Consortium if 
doing so would advance the national interest of the United States.
---------------------------------------------------------------------------

    \2\ Trusted Foreign Enterprises were referred to as National 
Champion Enterprises in the April 2026 CFP.
---------------------------------------------------------------------------

    On-Demand Consortia are also strongly encouraged to provide 
information relating to the telecommunications and energy 
infrastructure that will support the package. Specifically, applicants 
are encouraged to show that (1) applicable telecommunications 
infrastructure uses technology from trusted sources, meaning it does 
not rely on technology owned, controlled, or manufactured by entities 
of countries of concern as defined in the April 2026 CFP, and (2) 
sufficient energy sources, as appropriate, are or will be in place and 
operational to support the buyer's SI stack. Any such information will 
be favorably considered in the national interest determination under 
Section V of this notice.

III. Qualifying Opportunity

    A proposal from an On-Demand Consortium must be organized around a 
specific, qualifying public or private

- **Chinese actor (Storm-0940):** Microsoft tied this China state-aligned group to attacks on Microsoft 365 environments linked to ConnectWise Cloud Backup. - **Dates are inconsistent:** One source gives an October 21 account, but also refers to activity as early as September 2026, while another says the attackers had been using ARTEX since September. I could not confirm the exact timeline from primary Microsoft material, so check Microsoft's Threat Intelligence blog directly before relying on dates.

# Title: Attack Policy Selection can Mislead Monitor Evaluators
Authors: Charlie Griffin , Oliver Makins , Asa Cooper Stickland , Alessandro Abate , Yarin Gal , Abby D'Cruz , Xander Davies
View a PDF of the paper titled Attack Policy Selection can Mislead Monitor Evaluators, by Charlie Griffin and 6 other authors
View PDF
HTML (experimental)
Abstract: AI monitors, classifiers that flag dangerous behaviour by AI agents, are often evaluated against transcripts generated by attack policies acting as proxies for dangerous behaviour in deployment. We evaluate an ex-production OpenAI monitor as a case study and find that measured false negative rate is highly sensitive to both the method used to generate attack policies and the level of optimisation applied within that method. This rate ranged from 0.5\% to 20.8\% across optimisation levels of a single method (reinforcement learning), and from 6.4\% to 23.0\% across methods at their best observed optimisation level (optimised prompting vs.\ transcript editing). Every attack policy was developed against proxy monitors only: all reported results show attacks transferring to the held-out GPT-5.4 target monitor. Our results suggest that monitor evasion evaluations can easily mislead: an evaluation using only basic attack methods may give false confidence that a monitor is strong.
The sensitivity to attack-policy choice raises a problem: interpreting any particular result as evidence about deployment performance requires justification. The transcripts produced by attack policies are proxies for the dangerous behaviour a monitor must flag in deployment. These proxies can introduce visible artefacts, such as reasoning about a ``side task'' absent from the instructions shown to the monitor, that affect monitor judgements. Given the sensitivity above, the choice of proxy can change an evaluation's conclusion. Reading these results as evidence about deployment therefore requires a separate legitimacy argument for why the proxies are informative, including any justification of conservativeness. Making convincing arguments remains an open problem.

We test our setup in experiments where we compare a backdoored model with the base model from which it was fine-tuned. Our results show that incorporating the $J{+}{+}$-lens improves the weight-based method in all our settings, while the $J$-lens improves its ranks within single layers. Moreover, we show that output and activation based methods such as ADL and Diff Mining can easily break if the backdoored model is penalised during fine-tuning for giving the backdoor's words probability on clean inputs, whereas the weight-based methods are not affected. # Title: How Much Do Coding Agents Over-Edit, and Why? An Empirical Study of Unneeded Edits in Repository-Level Agent Patches
Authors: Aakash Goel , Benjamin Steenhoek , Yu Hu
View a PDF of the paper titled How Much Do Coding Agents Over-Edit, and Why? An Empirical Study of Unneeded Edits in Repository-Level Agent Patches, by Aakash Goel and 2 other authors
View PDF
HTML (experimental)
Abstract: Agent patches are larger than developers', which is widely read as over-editing. But patch size does not say whether the extra edits are needed, what they are, or where they come from. We introduce Delta Residue Attribution (DRA), which replays agent trajectories, traces every block (unit) of the final patch to the step that wrote it, reverts each unit, and reruns the task tests to decide whether the unit is needed. We apply DRA to 7,660 resolved GitHub Copilot CLI trajectories from 18 frontier models on SWE-bench Verified (6,728) and DeepSWE (932), and grade developer patches using the same method. Agent patches do change more lines than developers'; on SWE-bench Verified the majority of extra edits add tests (61%) and documentation (13%) while on DeepSWE, most extra edits are code (58%). On both benchmarks, agents' code is on average at least as necessary as developers' (mean $NP_{code}$ 0.887 vs. 0.864 on SWE-bench Verified, where 11 of 18 models leave less unneeded code than developers, and 0.797 vs. 0.785 on DeepSWE). On average, 11% of an agent patch's code units on SWE-bench Verified are still unneeded, and 89% of those change behavior. Debug steps write almost none of the unneeded code. Code necessity differs substantially by model; it is unrelated to resolve rate on SWE-bench Verified and negatively correlated with it on DeepSWE (Spearman -0.59, p = 0.01). On SWE-bench Verified, pruning with DRA using only the tests the agent can see (its own tests and the repository's) removes the majority of unneeded code but also some needed code (67% recall, 46% precision), and 89% of pruned patches still resolve the task; asking the agent to audit its own diff is more precise but less effective (36% recall, 66% precision). We recommend that benchmarks report code necessity next to resolve rate and that over-editing be addressed through model training and harness-level pruning.

# Title: FORK: Co-Evolving Safe Disclosure and Decision Skills Against Attackers Who Read Every Refusal
Authors: Hieu Man , Chao Shang , Rui Dong , Devang Kulshreshtha , Yanjun Qi , Sandesh Swamy
View a PDF of the paper titled FORK: Co-Evolving Safe Disclosure and Decision Skills Against Attackers Who Read Every Refusal, by Hieu Man and 5 other authors
View PDF
HTML (experimental)
Abstract: When a guardrail rejects an LLM agent's action, its message reaches any attacker observing the trajectory: a fixed refusal leaves benign users unable to recover, whereas an explanation can tell the attacker what to try next. We study this as safe disclosure: explaining rejections so that authorized tasks recover without increasing adaptive attack success. Safe disclosure depends on both the decision and the message: what the guardrail blocks and what it reveals to the agent and the attacker. Because hand-written rules alone cannot anticipate how adaptive attackers probe decisions or use messages, we introduce FORK, which co-evolves a guardrail's natural-language decision and disclosure skills with an attacker that reads every public message. Each exploited message and permissive decision gives FORK evidence for a gradient-free revision of its natural-language skill library. We evaluate FORK on four benchmarks. Averaged over three agents on FORK-World, FORK cuts attack success rate (ASR) under adaptive attack from 78.4% to 14.1% and keeps utility above 85%, outperforming baselines on both ASR and utility. Notably, on MT-AgentRisk, whose environments and tasks are unseen in training, FORK lowers ASR from 70.6% to 9.1% with 93.1% benign utility.

Abstract
-
When LLM agents verify each other’s work over a long interaction, they drift into collusion: they come to accept work without the evidence
that the verification protocol requires. Collusion is absent at the start and builds up episode by episode, which we trace to accurate
feedback accumulating in memory. An agent that follows the rule is told that its verdict was wrong whenever its peer
was right, so breaking the rule is the reward-maximizing choice, and agents talk themselves into it in their private reflections. Existing
mitigations leave the agents unchanged; we train the behavior out. PROVE (Protocol
Reinforcement from Verified Evidence) is a multi-agent reinforcement learning method that rewards verdicts by the evidence behind them
rather than by their outcome, and credits every call an agent makes, including the calls that solve its own task, with the outcome that call
controls. On Qwen3.6-27B, a LoRA adapter trained on six-episode interactions takes the collusion rate on held-out task sequences at the
original ten-episode horizon from 65.0% to 1.0%, with no detectable change in task success. Collusion that converged in every
interaction now converges in none, and the gain holds four episodes beyond the longest interaction seen in training. The trained 27B model
colludes less than every model evaluated in the original study, closed-weight frontier models included.

# Abstract.
AI coding agents write code faster than people can review it, so teams add AI reviewers. Reasoning models let such a reviewer trade cost for diligence through an effort setting. We asked how much effort a reviewer needs to catch plausible-but-wrong patches, which pass a benchmark’s tests but fail stronger ones. Claude Opus 5.5 (preregistered), Sonnet 5.5 and Haiku 5.5 (exploratory) each reviewed the same 90 agent-written Django patches from SWE-bench Verified at low, medium and high effort. By strengthened SWE-ABS tests, 55 patches were wrong and 35 correct. In every model, high effort accepted fewer wrong patches than low (false success .45 against .67 for Opus, .49 against .65 for Sonnet, .51 against .78 for Haiku), a supported difference for Opus and Haiku. For Opus, medium was non-inferior to high within 15 percentage points (difference .018, 95% CI [ − - .065, .108]) and cost 20% less, short of the preregistered 30%. For Sonnet and Haiku, medium cost 39% and 51% less than high but was not shown non-inferior. Opus at medium or high agreed best with the labels; Haiku at high cost about 8% as much per review as Opus at medium, accuracy difference unresolved. Exploratory coding showed that most rejections named the tested defect and that effort added such rejections. No setting is a strong gate: each accepted at least 45% of wrong patches. For 32 of the 55 wrong patches the issue may not require what the failing test checks; without them, neither accuracy hypothesis holds for any model.
# Keywords:
code review, large language models, LLM-as-a-judge, reasoning effort, patch correctness, SWE-bench
# 1. Introduction
Coding agents now produce code much faster than people do. In 806 open-source projects that adopted the Cursor agent, lines of code added rose by 281% in the first month, though the gain faded after two months ( He et al., 2026 ) ; in one project, a developer submitted as many agent-written pull requests in three days as they had submitted without an agent in the previous three years ( Li et al., 2025 ) . Review has not kept pace. In telemetry from more than 10,000 developers, the time spent reviewing each pull request rose 91% in teams with high AI adoption ( Faros AI, 2025 ) , and a study of agent-written pull requests reports a growing imbalance between how fast they are submitted and how fast they can be reviewed ( Li et al., 2025 ) . Review is becoming the bottleneck, and a common response is a second model that reviews each patch before merge. Trust My Bot (https://github.com/trustmybot/tmb ), an agent harness, gates every push this way. Such a gate is worth its cost only if it rejects broken patches without rejecting good ones.
Reasoning models expose an effort setting that controls how much work the model does before it answers. Claude Opus 5.5 offers five levels, with medium as the default ( Anthropic, 2026a ; Anthropic, 2026b ) . Effort shapes all output, thinking, tool calls and text, and is not a strict token budget ( Anthropic, 2026a ) . More effort costs more; whether it also gives better verdicts sets the price of a review gate. The answer may differ by model: a smaller model costs less per review and may need more effort to reach the same verdicts.
Measuring a reviewer needs a reference standard. SWE-bench Verified pairs GitHub issues with tests that people screened as fair ( Chowdhury et al., 2024 ; Jimenez et al., 2024 ) , but those tests are weak: SWE-ABS strengthens them ( Yu et al., 2026 ) . Its paper reports that the stronger tests reject 19.78% of the passing patches of its top 30 agents ( Yu et al., 2026 ) , and by our count its released verdicts reject 18.6% of the passing patches of all 39 agents (2,682 of 14,446) ( OpenAgentEval, 2026 ) . A patch that passes the Verified tests but fails SWE-ABS is plausible but wrong . The benchmark counts it as solved, and a review gate exists to catch it.
We report a paired experiment in which three Claude 5.5 models, Opus, Sonnet and Haiku, reviewed the same 90 patches at low, medium and high effort. The Opus study was preregistered and is confirmatory; the Sonnet and Haiku studies are exploratory. The reviewer setup was fixed; only effort and the model varied. This paper is the first in a series of studies of AI code review; later studies vary a note from the patch’s author, the reviewer’s skills and voting among several reviewers. We asked:
- •
RQ1. In each model, does effort change how often the reviewer accepts wrong patches (false success) and rejects correct ones (false alarm)?
- •
RQ2. In each model, is medium effort as good as high on false success, and materially cheaper?

AI companies rely on monitoring systems to flag dangerous behaviour by AI agents, and report monitor evasion evaluations [ 3 , 2 , 16 ] that try to assess whether agents can cause harm without being flagged. Control-style evaluations [ 8 ] measure a monitor’s false negative rate (FNR, also known as “miss rate”) on transcripts depicting attempts at harmful behaviour. These evaluations have two components: a control task specifies a user-requested main task and a harmful side task in an evaluation environment; an attack policy generates side-task attempts as proxies for dangerous agent behaviour.
We evaluate an ex-production OpenAI monitor as a case study ( Section 1 ) and find that measured FNR is highly sensitive to both the method used to generate attack policies and the level of optimisation applied within that method ( Section 2 ).
We hold the deployment scenario and control tasks fixed and vary only the attack policy. FNR ranged from 0.5% to 20.8% across optimisation levels of a single method (reinforcement learning), and from 6.4% to 23.0% across methods at their best observed optimisation level (optimised prompting vs. transcript editing). Every attack policy was developed against proxy monitors only: all reported FNRs show attacks transferring to the held-out GPT-5.4 target monitor. Our results suggest that monitor evasion evaluations can easily mislead: an evaluation using only basic attack methods may give false confidence that a monitor is strong ( Fig. 1 ).
Left: running only the lightest optimisation level of three methods (the basic prompt, the first round of prompt optimisation and the first reinforcement learning (RL) checkpoint) finds FNRs of at most 5.1%. Right: running every optimisation level of all four methods finds FNRs up to 23.0%. All attacks were developed against proxy monitors; GPT-5.4 was held out. Bars: 95% bootstrap intervals. Both evaluations use the same 30 control tasks.
This paper concerns the third step, monitor evasion and specifically monitor evasion evaluations that follow the methodology of Greenblatt et al. [8] , which we call control-style evaluations . These measure a monitor’s FNR on attack transcripts, each produced by applying an attack policy to a control task.
Anthropic [ 3 , Section 6.6.4.2] , Google DeepMind [ 7 , Section 3.4.5.4] and OpenAI [ 15 , Section 4.2.2.2] have all used control-style evaluations in their recent system cards. Our work highlights a challenge in using these evaluations: different attack policy generation methods can have a large influence on measured FNR.
Our deployment scenario involves Qwen 3.8 27B (xhigh reasoning) running as an internal agent at a frontier AI developer, completing tasks such as writing infrastructure code. The agent is deployed with an asynchronous monitor : after the agent finishes a rollout, the monitor reads the full transcript—actions and reasoning—and flags suspicious transcripts for human review. We target an ex-production OpenAI monitor , similar to Williams et al. [23] , using GPT-5.4 with xhigh reasoning as the monitor model with a prompt supplied by OpenAI.
Our behavioural problem statement, centring uncertainty about dangerous behaviour given a fixed model, is a departure from past work, including our own. That work centres uncertainty about whether the agent is ‘trying’ to subvert safety measures (“intentional subversion” [ 8 ] ), and so measures the agent’s capability to do so if it were: “a conservative upper bound of the sabotage abilities” of the agent [ 19 ] . Our target estimand is therefore forward-looking: the probability that, if this agent were deployed, the monitor fails to flag the transcript containing its first dangerous action.
Although on-policy for the previously deployed model, this behaviour is still off-policy for a new target agent model. Using in-the-wild behaviour from the target agent in more secure settings also leaves a potential mismatch with its intended deployment environment. More broadly, assessing whether monitors would catch the most dangerous attacks before they happen may require evaluating them without representative real examples of those attacks.
We evaluate monitors using attack policies produced by four attack generation methods: basic prompting, optimised prompting, reinforcement learning, and transcript editing . We present results in IaC here, and show results in LinuxArena in Appendix F . Throughout, the GPT-5.4 target monitor is held out: all attack development and optimisation used proxy monitors, so the FNRs we report measure transfer to a monitor the attacks never received feedback from.

We also improve existing weight and activation based methods by incorporating the J J -lens and its refinement, the J + + J{+}{+} -lens. We test our setup in experiments where we compare a backdoored model with the base model from which it was fine-tuned. Our results show that incorporating the J + + J{+}{+} -lens improves the weight-based method in all our settings, while the J J -lens improves its ranks within single layers. The strongest single method is Δ ​ W ​ J + + \Delta WJ{+}{+} , the weight difference decoded through the J + + J{+}{+} -lens of the base model, which ranks a token naming the backdoor among its first ten tokens in 11 of our 12 settings. Moreover, we show that output and activation based methods such as ADL and Diff Mining can easily break if the backdoored model is penalised during fine-tuning for giving the backdoor’s words probability on clean inputs, whereas the weight-based methods are not affected. Conversely, permuting the hidden units or training only the layers that read the residual stream hides the backdoor from the weight-based methods but not from ADL and Diff Mining. No single method resists both attacks.
In many cases the model that the suspect was fine-tuned from, the base , is public, and the auditor can ask what the fine-tune changed, a question known as model diffing [ 3 ] . Several recent methods answer it without knowing the trigger or the training data, by comparing the weights (Watch the Weights [ 4 ] ), the activations on ordinary text (the Activation Difference Lens, ADL, of Minder et al. [ 5 ] ) or the output probabilities (Diff Mining [ 6 ] ) of the two models. Each of them was evaluated on its own organisms, against its own reference and with its own metric (Section 2.2 ), so it is hard to determine which of them works best on which kind of backdoor, or why.
We bring these methods into one form (Figure 1 ): compute a difference between the suspect and a reference, extract a few directions from it at each layer in the model’s hidden space, and decode every direction into a ranked list of vocabulary tokens, which we call a token readout . For a backdoor that makes the model talk about whales, we expect a good method to return readouts with whale at the top. When taking weight differences, we take the directions of Watch the Weights [ 4 ] and decode them into tokens instead of using them as monitors, and call the resulting method Δ ​ W \Delta W . The activation based method ADL is implemented based on how it was published [ 5 ] . We can therefore run all methods on the same backdoored models, against the same reference, and score them in the same way, by how high the backdoor’s target word ranks in their readouts. This score is a yardstick for comparing methods and not a detector. It needs a target word chosen in advance, which a real auditor does not have. An auditor works with the readouts themselves, reading them, grouping related tokens by meaning, or handing them to an LLM as ADL does. A readout that scores well is a good starting point for any of these, and we save the full readouts of every method so that such analyses can be built on them.

# Attack Policy Selection can Mislead Monitor Evaluators

Charlie Griffin

  
Oliver Makins

  
Asa Cooper Stickland

Affiliation: Alessandro Abate, Yarin Gal, Abby D’Cruz, Xander Davies

AI companies rely on monitoring systems to flag dangerous behaviour by AI agents, and report monitor evasion evaluations [ 3 , 2 , 16 ] that try to assess whether agents can cause harm without being flagged. Control-style evaluations [ 8 ] measure a monitor’s false negative rate (FNR, also known as “miss rate”) on transcripts depicting attempts at harmful behaviour. These evaluations have two components: a control task specifies a user-requested main task and a harmful side task in an evaluation environment; an attack policy generates side-task attempts as proxies for dangerous agent behaviour.

We evaluate an ex-production OpenAI monitor as a case study ( Section 1 ) and find that measured FNR is highly sensitive to both the method used to generate attack policies and the level of optimisation applied within that method ( Section 2 ).
We hold the deployment scenario and control tasks fixed and vary only the attack policy. FNR ranged from 0.5% to 20.8% across optimisation levels of a single method (reinforcement learning), and from 6.4% to 23.0% across methods at their best observed optimisation level (optimised prompting vs. transcript editing). Every attack policy was developed against proxy monitors only: all reported FNRs show attacks transferring to the held-out GPT-5.4 target monitor. Our results suggest that monitor evasion evaluations can easily mislead: an evaluation using only basic attack methods may give false confidence that a monitor is strong ( Fig. 1 ).

Figure 1: A narrowly optimised evaluation can make the monitor look robust.
Left: running only the lightest optimisation level of three methods (the basic prompt, the first round of prompt optimisation and the first reinforcement learning (RL) checkpoint) finds FNRs of at most 5.1%. Right: running every optimisation level of all four methods finds FNRs up to 23.0%. All attacks were developed against proxy monitors; GPT-5.4 was held out. Bars: 95% bootstrap intervals. Both evaluations use the same 30 control tasks.

The sensitivity to attack-policy choice raises a problem: interpreting any particular result as evidence about deployment performance requires justification. The transcripts produced by attack policies are proxies for the dangerous behaviour a monitor must flag in deployment ( Section 3.1 ). These proxies can introduce visible artefacts, such as reasoning about a “side task” absent from the instructions shown to the monitor, that affect monitor judgements ( Section 3.2 ). Given the sensitivity above, the choice of proxy can change an evaluation’s conclusion. Reading measured FNR as evidence about deployment therefore requires a separate legitimacy argument for why the proxies are informative, including any justification of conservativeness. Making convincing arguments remains an open problem ( Section 3.3 ).

Linear attention offers an efficient solution for long-sequence modeling via linear complexity and fixed-size recurrent states. Gated DeltaNet-2 (GDN-2) introduces independent channel-wise control over erasure and writing, enhancing state-update expressiveness and in-context retrieval, yet it suffers from training failures during long-context training. We trace these failures to the asymmetry between reading and modification directions during erasure, which yields non-normal erase operators whose directional gains accumulate across tokens, triggering exponential state growth even without new writes. To resolve this, we propose Stable GDN-2 , employing symmetric erasure to ensure non-expansive state propagation and decay-regulated residual writing to preserve writing flexibility. Theoretically, we establish an O ⁡ ( T ) O(\sqrt{T}) upper bound on recurrent state growth while retaining chunkwise parallel computation. Experiments on 1.6B parameter models show that Stable GDN-2 achieves stable training alongside improved long-context retrieval. Compared to GDN-2, it boosts the 128K average RULER score by 6.80 points in the recurrent setting and average accuracy across nine downstream tasks by 0.62 points in the hybrid setting.

The government's National Cyber Action Plan has been delayed again. Photo: Alexander Martin

# UK’s long-awaited National Cyber Action Plan delayed until December
Britain has again delayed the launch of its National Cyber Action Plan, the government’s long-awaited strategy for defending the wider economy against state-backed and criminal hackers, according to multiple people familiar with the matter.
The document, originally conceived as a national cyber strategy, was first due to be published by the end of 2025. After initial delays it was rebranded as an action plan and was close to publication in July this year before being postponed amid Keir Starmer’s resignation.
Officials, who had planned to publish the document in mid-November, now aim to unveil it on December 9 according to several sources, speaking to Recorded Future News on condition of anonymity.
The reasons for the latest delay are unclear. A government spokesperson declined to comment on the timing but said ministers remained committed to publishing the plan.
The latest delay follows an influential cross-party House of Lords committee warning that the government “appears complacent” about “potentially catastrophic risks,” including cyberattacks from Russia, China and Iran.
In a report published last week, the National Resilience Committee found Britain was dangerously underprepared for crises which could cascade across the economy, with disruption spilling over multiple sectors and disrupting the everyday lives of millions of people.
Baroness Northover, a Liberal Democrat member of the committee, told Recorded Future News that the country could not afford more uncertainty or drift. “This situation is unacceptable at a time of significant and escalating risk,” she said. “We must act urgently. The cost of inaction is enormous.”
“Further absence of an overarching National Cyber Action Plan, aimed at defending the economy against state-backed and criminal hacking, is not just frustrating, it is serious,” she said.
“The UK has got to keep pace with threats. Delay and avoidance is simply not an option and underlines the Committee’s point that the UK remains seriously exposed and underprepared for very significant events, and our vulnerability is current, active and acute on many fronts.”

# No dither but delay
Successive delays to cybersecurity legislation and policy announcements have contributed to a perception that the issue is a low political priority, despite its growing importance to Britain’s economic and national security.
The Cyber Security and Resilience Bill , an update to the country's critical-infrastructure cyber laws, took more than four years to reach Parliament and is now not expected to be enforced until 2028 — a decade on from the NIS Regulations it was written to replace.
The core provisions of the CSRB had already been completed back in 2022 under Rishi Sunak, whose government incorrectly described the laws as “updated” before failing to include them in that year's King's Speech setting out the government’s parliamentary agenda and leaving the draft bill ultimately unintroduced to parliament.
When Starmer's government first moved to bring the bill forward in September 2025, it was then delayed again amid a cabinet reshuffle .
Separately, a set of ransomware proposals — mandatory reporting for all victims, a licensing regime for extortion payments and a ban on ransoms for critical infrastructure operators — was due to go out to consultation in mid-2024, before being scuppered when Sunak called a general election.
Officials argue that the delays belie the substantial amount of work underway in Westminster.
The government is expected to bring forward a new National Security Bill next year to reform the Computer Misuse Act — although some fear the reforms as proposed would fail to protect security researchers — as well as finally set the ransomware proposals on the statute books.
In last month’s budget, the government committed £120 million ($159 million) over four years to the AI Security Institute and a further £40 million ($53 million) to establish a National Agentic Security Unit to address the threats posed by AI agents acting autonomously.
Another £70 million ($93 million) was earmarked for an AI-powered vulnerability hunting center at the National Cyber Security Centre (NCSC), with £60 million ($79 million) allocated to the first phase of Cyber Shield, a national defense system that would use AI agents to find and fix security weaknesses across government and critical infrastructure networks.
Potentially more consequential for the technology industry was a commitment , buried among the budget announcements, that the government would consult next year on “where liability for cyber breaches should sit.”
Ministers have also launched a voluntary Cyber Resilience Pledge, seeking commitments from British businesses to put cybersecurity on the boardroom agenda and better manage their supply-chain risks. The government describes the pledge as a central pillar of the National Cyber Action Plan.

# National Cyber Action Plan
The plan’s contents have not been officially disclosed. Recorded Future News understands it will include three pillars focusing on Threat, Growth and Resilience.

**Shadowserver: Agentic AI Attack Frameworks in the Wild**
*Published November 25, 2026*

Shadowserver has begun daily scanning for publicly exposed instances of 15 autonomous AI attack frameworks, which let LLM agents perform reconnaissance and exploitation with little human involvement. Some of these tools are built for authorized penetration testing, so exposure does not always indicate malicious use.

**Exposure (as of November 23, 2026)**
- About 4,200 exposed instances, up from just under 3,700 the day before.
- Nearly half were in Asia, over a third in North America, and most of the rest in Europe.
- ARTEX accounted for roughly 70% of instances on most days. AntiFox, a fork of ARTEX, grew fastest to about 200.
- PentestCode rose to over 600 on November 23, driving the week's peak.

**Honeypot activity (November 9–23, 2026)**
- More than 80 IP addresses generated over 10,000 events. A handful of IPs accounted for most of them.
- Nearly nine in ten attacking IPs were fingerprinted as ARTEX Gateway.
- IPs geolocated in more than 20 countries, concentrated in the United States and Hong Kong. Almost all were on cloud networks, so location may reflect hosting rather than operator location.
- About six in ten IPs attempted to relay traffic through the sensors, with over 40% of relay requests targeting payment, banking, and crypto services.
- Roughly one in ten IPs looked for credentials such as .env files and Git metadata, or tried default logins.
- About one in ten IPs sent exploit or injection payloads, most often targeting Metabase CVE-2023-38646.
- Nearly half of IPs were active for less than an hour in total, while a few ran around the clock.

**Key recommendations**
- Subscribe to Shadowserver's daily network reports.
- Verify whether any detected framework deployments are authorized. Restrict access or isolate unauthorized ones.
- Consider blocking known framework-running IPs, while avoiding authorized testing infrastructure and reviewing blocklists regularly, since hosting IPs are often reassigned.
- Rate-limit and alert on rapid, iterative probing, with alerts handled outside business hours where possible.

Neoclouds are being told they won't be able to purchase Nvidia chips if any of the computing capacity will be rented by Chinese companies, sources told CNBC.
It comes after a new rule restricting remote access to artificial-intelligence semiconductors was announced by the Trump administration on Nov. 16.

Chip sellers communicated the messaging to neoclouds after the announcement, which seeks to close an export controls loophole allowing Chinese companies to rent access to Nvidia's most advanced chips when hosted in data centers overseas, two people familiar with the situation told CNBC. The people asked not to be named when discussing private information.
The interim final rule was announced by the Department of Commerce's Bureau of Industry and Security, or BIS, and came into effect on Nov. 19. Previously imposed export controls have effectively banned the sale of the most advanced Nvidia chips to Chinese companies and their import into China.
Prior to the new rule's announcement, Nvidia had said it would not sell its chips to customers renting more than 50% of the graphics processing units, or GPUs, to Chinese companies, CNBC reported.
The new rule impacts the full supply chain, from the companies selling Nvidia chips to the neoclouds who rent access to computing power. Neocloud stocks have come under renewed pressure lately as investors questioned the sustainability of the AI boom.
Nvidia and the U.S. Department of Commerce's Bureau of Industry and Security did not immediately respond to a request for comment.

# Closing 'loopholes'
The change has prompted Nvidia chip sellers to look for new buyers of the semiconductor giant's GPUs, CNBC reported on Wednesday, citing three people familiar with the matter. Two of those people said it appeared chip sellers were seeking to offload GPUs because they were originally for use in data centers through which Chinese companies would rent access.
